subject: rla
title: The Extended Response II: Organizing, Revising, and Full RLA Review
objectives: You will organize an extended response into an introduction with a thesis, body paragraphs, and a conclusion, following a 45-minute plan.
You will build body paragraphs (Point, Evidence, Explain, Link) that use specific, accurate evidence from both passages and explain why it is strong or weak.
You will revise for ideas and organization, then edit for grammar, usage, and mechanics, in the last minutes.
You will score sample responses with the GED's three traits and explain what moves a response from low to high.
You will review the full range of RLA skills: informational and literary reading, language editing, and evaluating arguments.

slides.title: The Extended Response II: Organizing, Revising, and Full RLA Review
slides.board:
Week 10 · Reasoning Through Language Arts

Today you will:

  • Follow a 45-minute plan and a response blueprint
  • Build PEEL body paragraphs with evidence from both passages
  • Revise, then edit, in the last seven minutes

Plan: Warm-up · Plan and organize · Body paragraphs · Revise and edit · Scoring · Full review · GED questions · Recap

notes.say: This is the last week of the course, and the essay is where everything we have practiced comes together: main idea, evidence, argument, comparing texts, and grammar. Last week the student learned to judge two arguments and write a thesis. Today they turn that thesis into a complete, organized response inside 45 minutes, and then we sweep through the whole RLA test. Tell them plainly: a full 45-minute response does not fit in this hour, so today we practice each part, and they write a full timed response on their own this week.
ask: What part of the essay worries you most: getting started, finding evidence, or finishing on time? (expected: any honest answer; note it and return to it during the lesson)

slides.title: Week 9 review: judging evidence
slides.board:
Answer out loud.

  1. Name the five evidence questions.
  2. Which is stronger evidence, and why? (a) “A neighbor says the new bike lanes cause accidents.” (b) “City crash reports show 12 bike crashes on Elm Street the year before the lanes and 5 the year after.”
  3. Name the red flag: “Everyone at my gym agrees: keep the pool open.”
  4. Which thesis judges the support? (a) “The library should stay open late; reading matters.” (b) “Reyes's argument is better supported because she cites usage data, while Lamb relies on one complaint.”
steps: 1. Source (who, and are they reliable?), specific (numbers, names, dates?), relevant (does it prove this claim?), sufficient (enough, or one story?), fair (does it deal with the other side?).
2. (b): a named, official source with measured numbers. (a) is one unnamed person's opinion.
3. Bandwagon: it claims the idea is right because many people believe it.
4. (b) judges whose support is stronger and previews why. (a) argues the issue.

notes.say: These four questions review last week's skills, which today's lesson builds on. Give the student about a minute each and make them give a reason for every answer, because the reason is exactly what goes into a body paragraph. If they cannot name all five evidence questions, give the first letter of each as a hint.
notes.answer: 1. Source, specific, relevant, sufficient, fair. 2. (b), because it is specific, measured, and from official crash reports. 3. Bandwagon (appeal to popular opinion). 4. (b); (a) gives an opinion on the issue instead of judging the arguments.
notes.watch: On question 4, a student who picks (a) is still arguing the issue. Ask, “Does this sentence say whose evidence is better?” This is the single most costly essay mistake, so name it now.

slides.title: Week 9 review: thesis and rubric
slides.board:
Answer out loud.

  1. What does PEEL stand for?
  2. What exactly does the GED essay prompt ask you to decide?
  3. Fix this thesis: “I agree with Okafor because pay should be public.”
  4. How many scoring traits are there, and how many points is each worth?
steps: 1. Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.
2. Which of the two positions is better supported, using specific evidence from both passages. Not which side you agree with.
3. Sample: “Okafor's argument is better supported because she relies on measured results from a real pilot, while Whitlock relies on one story.”
4. Three traits, each worth 0 to 2 points.

notes.say: Quick recall before we build. The student needs PEEL and the exact task wording at their fingertips, because everything today hangs on them. For question 3, push for a full rewrite, not just “take out I agree.”
notes.answer: 1. Point, Evidence, Explain, Link. 2. Which position is better supported, using evidence from both passages. 3. Any thesis that names the better-supported writer and gives a reason about evidence. 4. Three traits, 0–2 points each.
notes.watch: If the student's rewrite in question 3 still says “because pay should be public,” it is still about the issue. The “because” must name evidence: results, data, answering critics, one story, predictions.

slides.title: The 45-minute plan
slides.board:
MinutesJob
0–8Read: prompt, then both passages. Mark claims, best evidence, weak spots.
8–13Plan: decide, write the thesis, list 2–3 body points.
13–38Draft: intro (3), body paragraphs (6–7 each), conclusion (3).
38–45Revise (3), then edit (4).

Behind? Shorten a body paragraph. Never cut the conclusion or the edit.

notes.say: The biggest reason good readers score low on the essay is that they run out of time. A plan protects them. Walk through each block and stress that it is a guide, not a cage: if reading takes ten minutes, take a minute from each body paragraph, never from the conclusion or the edit. A finished response with a short conclusion beats a long, unfinished one.
ask: If the plan says 13 to 38 for drafting, how many minutes is that? (expected: 25)
What do you cut if you fall behind? (expected: part of a body paragraph, not the conclusion or the edit)
notes.watch: Some students want to skip planning and start typing at minute 1. Point out that five minutes of planning saves far more than five minutes of rewriting.

slides.title: A five-minute plan
slides.board:
Passage A (Okafor): Harlow should require employers with 15+ workers to post pay ranges.
Passage B (Whitlock): Keep the city out of job ads.

Build a T-chart, then a thesis and outline.
steps: Okafor: pilot, 40 employers: 22% fewer applicants who later refused the pay; 41 → 33 days to fill a job. County review: men/women starting-pay gap about half as large. Answers critics: under-15 exemption, range not exact salary, 37 of 40 kept posting.
Whitlock: one story (press operator); prediction that workers “will demand raises”; slippery slope (city will set pay); vague “many business owners I know.” Fair point: pilot employers volunteered.
Thesis: Okafor's argument is better supported because she relies on measured results and answers her critics, while Whitlock relies on one story and predictions he never supports.
Outline: Body 1, Okafor's pilot and county data. Body 2, Whitlock's anecdote, prediction, slippery slope. Body 3, his volunteer point and why it does not outweigh her evidence.

notes.say: Model this out loud, thinking as you go. Fill Okafor's column, then Whitlock's, then decide. Point out that the decision comes from the chart: one column is full of measured results and answers to critics; the other is one story, predictions, and a vague appeal. Show that the outline falls straight out of the chart.
ask: Which column has more measured results? (expected: Okafor's)
What is Whitlock's best point? (expected: the pilot employers volunteered)

slides.title: The response blueprint
slides.board:
1. Introduction: issue · both writers and positions · thesis last
  2. Body 1: stronger writer's best evidence and why it is strong
  3. Body 2: weaker writer's evidence and why it is weak
  4. Body 3 (if time): concede the weaker side's best point, then answer it
  5. Conclusion: restate the judgment in new words; sum up; no new evidence

Delete: “I think,” your own opinion on the issue, stories from your life.

notes.say: This is the skeleton every high-scoring response shares, and it maps right onto Trait 2. The introduction ends with the thesis so the reader knows exactly what the body will prove. Body paragraphs cover both writers, because the prompt says to analyze both positions. The concession paragraph is optional but powerful. The conclusion is short and adds nothing new.
ask: Where does the thesis go? (expected: last sentence of the introduction)
Why must you write about the weaker writer too? (expected: the prompt says to analyze both positions)

slides.title: Where does it go?
slides.board:
Label each sentence: Introduction, Body, Conclusion, or Delete.

  1. Okafor reports that 37 of the 40 pilot employers planned to keep posting ranges after the program ended.
  2. The two writers disagree about whether Harlow should require pay ranges in job ads.
  3. I once applied for a job that paid way less than I expected, so I agree with Okafor.
  4. Taken together, Okafor's data and her answer to critics make hers the stronger argument.
steps: 1. Body: specific evidence, credited to Okafor.
2. Introduction: frames the issue and both sides.
3. Delete: personal experience and opinion on the issue; the task is to judge the arguments.
4. Conclusion: sums up the judgment (“Taken together…”).

notes.say: The student leads; you reveal each answer only after they commit and give a reason. Spend the most time on sentence 3. It feels supportive of Okafor, but it is personal experience, and it is the mistake that costs the most on Trait 1.
ask: Why does sentence 3 get deleted even though it agrees with the stronger writer? (expected: it is personal experience, not evidence from the passages)
notes.watch: A student who keeps sentence 3 thinks agreeing with the stronger writer is the goal. Reframe: “The scorer is asking whose evidence is better, not whose side you are on.”

slides.title: PEEL with specific evidence
slides.board:
Point: one claim about the quality of support
Evidence: short exact quote or precise paraphrase, credited
Explain: why it is strong or weak
Link: back to the thesis

VagueSpecific
Okafor has a lot of facts.Okafor reports that the average time to fill a job fell from 41 days to 33 days.

Verbs: reports, argues, cites, predicts, claims

notes.say: Every body paragraph follows PEEL. The Explain step is where the points live: quoting without explaining is just copying. Specific evidence names the writer and uses the passage's own numbers or words, and it must be accurate; a wrong number tells the scorer you did not check. Teach the attribution verbs; “claims” is handy for weak evidence, as in “Whitlock claims that many owners agree.”
ask: Which PEEL step do writers skip most often? (expected: Explain)
Why is a misquoted number worse than no number? (expected: it shows you did not check, and it is inaccurate evidence)

slides.title: Vague to specific
slides.board:
Before: “Okafor shows that pay ranges are fair. She has good evidence about this and it proves her point.”

Make it specific, then explain it.
steps: Point: “Okafor also argues that pay ranges make hiring fairer.”

Evidence: “She cites a review of hiring records by the Marsh County Labor Office, which found that the gap between men's and women's starting pay was about half as large at employers that posted ranges.”
Explain: “Because this finding comes from actual hiring records rather than opinions, it gives readers solid reason to accept her claim.”
What changed: a clear point, a named source, the passage's own finding, and a reason the evidence is strong.

notes.say: Think aloud: which evidence, from where, and why is it good? Go to paragraph 3 of Passage A and use its exact finding. Then add the Explain step. Show the student that the after version is longer only because it actually says something.
ask: What does “it proves her point” fail to tell the reader? (expected: what the evidence is and why it is strong)

slides.title: Build a PEEL paragraph on Whitlock
slides.board:
Evidence to use: Whitlock claims a posted range “locks both sides in.” His support: the story of one press operator he hired last spring, who he says “might have” skipped the job if he had posted a range.

Together: write the Point, Evidence, Explain, and Link.
steps: Point: “Whitlock's argument rests on much weaker support than Okafor's.”
Evidence: “To show that a posted range ‘locks both sides in,’ he describes hiring a single press operator.”
Explain: “One hire at one shop cannot show what will happen across a city, and his claim that she ‘might have’ skipped the job is only a guess.”
Link: “Because his main claim rests on one anecdote, his position is the less convincing of the two.”

notes.say: Build this paragraph with the student one step at a time. Ask for each piece, accept any version that does the job, and then reveal the model step. Keep pressing on Explain: why is one story weak evidence for a citywide rule?
ask: What kind of evidence is a single story? (expected: an anecdote)
Why is “might have” a weak spot? (expected: it is a guess about what could have happened, not something that did)
notes.answer: Model: “Whitlock's argument rests on much weaker support than Okafor's. To show that a posted range ‘locks both sides in,’ he describes hiring a single press operator. One hire at one shop cannot show what will happen across a city, and his claim that she ‘might have’ skipped the job is only a guess. Because his main claim rests on one anecdote, his position is the less convincing of the two.”
notes.watch: Students often stop after Evidence (“He tells a story about a press operator.”). Ask, “So what? Why does that make his argument weak?” until they produce the Explain sentence.

slides.title: Concede and answer
slides.board:
Concede: “To be fair, [weaker writer] raises one reasonable point: …”

Answer: “However, …” show why it does not change your judgment:

  • it has no evidence behind it, or
  • the other writer already answers it, or
  • it is small next to the evidence on the other side.

A concession shows you weighed both positions. It never switches sides.

notes.say: The prompt says to analyze both positions. The strongest responses go one step further: they admit the weaker writer's best point and then answer it. That shows the scorer real evaluation, which lifts Trait 1. Make clear that conceding is not surrendering: the paragraph must end with the thesis still standing.
ask: What is the risk if you concede and do not answer? (expected: it sounds like you changed sides, which weakens the thesis)

slides.title: Answering Whitlock's best point
slides.board:
Whitlock (paragraph 4): the 40 pilot employers volunteered, so they were already comfortable posting pay. Their experience “tells us nothing” about what happens when every business must follow the rule.

Write the concession paragraph.
steps: Concede: “To be fair, Whitlock raises one reasonable point: the pilot employers volunteered, so their results might not match those of employers who are required to post pay.”
Answer, part 1: “However, he offers no evidence that the results would be different, and saying the pilot ‘tells us nothing’ overstates the problem.”
Answer, part 2: “Okafor also shows that the ordinance was written with small businesses in mind: it exempts those with fewer than fifteen workers and requires only a range.”
Result: the fair point is admitted, and the thesis still stands.

notes.say: Model the paragraph in three moves: concede, point out what is missing, then use the other passage. Note that Whitlock overstates his point (“tells us nothing”), which is itself worth naming.
ask: Which word shows Whitlock overstating his point? (expected: “nothing,” as in “tells us nothing”)

slides.title: The last seven minutes
slides.board:
1. Revise (about 3 min)

  • Thesis clear? Judges the support?
  • Each body paragraph starts with a point?
  • Every piece of evidence explained?
  • Any “I think” or personal story? Delete.

2. Edit (about 4 min)

  • Fragments, run-ons, comma splices
  • Subject-verb agreement
  • their/there/they're · its/it's · then/than · to/too · a lot
  • Capitals for names and titles
  • Exact quotes and numbers

notes.say: Revise first, then edit. Revising fixes the big things that cost the most points: the thesis, the points, the explanations, anything off task. Editing fixes the small things. If you fix commas in a sentence you later delete, that time is wasted. Also remind the student that the response box has basic tools like cut, copy, and paste but no spell check, so their eyes are the only checker.
ask: Why revise before you edit? (expected: big problems cost more points, and you might delete sentences you would otherwise have edited)
notes.watch: Many students never reach the edit because they draft until 44:59. Practice the “38-minute alarm” until it is automatic.

slides.title: A seven-minute fix
slides.board:
Draft conclusion:

In conclusion Okafor is right and Whitlock is wrong. Pay ranges is a good idea and the city council should pass it. Their is no reason not too.
steps: Revise first (big): it judges the issue (“is right,” “good idea”) instead of the support. Rewrite it to restate the thesis and the reasons.
Then edit (small): comma after “In conclusion”; “Pay ranges is” → are; “city council” → City Council; “Their” → There; “too” → to.

Revised: “In conclusion, Okafor's argument is the better supported of the two. She backs her claims with results from a real pilot and a review of hiring records, while Whitlock depends on one story and predictions he never supports.”

notes.say: Model the order out loud: revise first, then edit, then show the final. Point out that if the student had only edited, they would have polished a conclusion that still argues the wrong thing.
ask: How many edits did the draft need? (expected: five)
Which problem was bigger, the edits or the revision? (expected: the revision; it was arguing the wrong thing)

slides.title: Revise, then edit, together
slides.board:
Whitlock's argument is not as good. He talks about a worker he hired and he thinks the range will lock people in. He also says employees will want raises which is a problem for there business. Its just a prediction. Alot of business owners agree with him though.

First revise (4 problems), then edit (5 errors).
steps: Revise: (1) vague point (“not as good”); (2) vague evidence (“talks about a worker”); (3) no explanation of why one story is weak; (4) “Alot of business owners agree” repeats his vague claim as fact instead of judging it.
Edit: comma before “and” joining two sentences; comma before “which”; there → their; Its → It's (or “This is”); Alot → A lot.

Model: “Whitlock's argument rests on much weaker support. To show that a posted range ‘locks both sides in,’ he describes hiring one press operator, but one hire at one shop cannot show what will happen across a city. He also predicts that employees ‘will demand raises,’ yet he gives no numbers or examples. Finally, his claim that ‘many business owners I know agree’ is vague, because he never says who they are or how many.”

notes.say: Work through this paragraph together. Ask for revision problems first, and do not accept any edits until the big problems are named. Then hunt for the five editing errors. Finally, reveal the model revision.
ask: What is wrong with ending on “Alot of business owners agree with him though”? (expected: it accepts Whitlock's vague claim as fact instead of evaluating it)
notes.answer: Revise: vague point, vague evidence, missing explanation, accepting a weak claim as fact. Edit: comma before “and”; comma before “which”; their; It's; A lot. Model revision as shown in the last step.
notes.watch: Students tend to jump straight to the spelling errors. Hold them to the order: revise first.

slides.title: How the essay is scored
slides.board:
Trait (0–2 each)Scorers look for
1 Arguments and use of evidenceA position on which argument is better supported; specific evidence from both passages; explanation
2 Development and organizationIntro, body, conclusion; developed ideas; logical order; transitions; formal tone
3 Clarity and standard EnglishClear, varied sentences; correct grammar, usage, mechanics

A few minor errors are expected in a 45-minute draft.

notes.say: Trained scorers give 0, 1, or 2 on each trait. Map today's lesson onto them: specific, explained evidence is Trait 1; the blueprint and transitions are Trait 2; the edit pass is Trait 3. Reassure the student that scorers know this is a timed first draft, so a few minor errors that do not get in the way of meaning will not sink Trait 3. But a response that argues only personal opinion, or copies the passages without analysis, scores low on Trait 1 however polished it is.
ask: Which trait does PEEL's Explain step help most? (expected: Trait 1)
Which trait does the edit pass protect? (expected: Trait 3)

slides.title: Scoring a low response
slides.board:
I think pay ranges are a good idea. When I was looking for work I applied to a warehouse job and it paid way less then I needed. Okafor is right about that. Whitlock just wants to keep his workers pay low. Businesses should be honest. So the city should pass it.

Score it trait by trait.
steps: Trait 1, low (0): argues the issue (“pay ranges are a good idea”); support is a personal story; nothing specific from either passage; “Whitlock just wants to keep his workers pay low” attacks the writer and is not in Passage B.
Trait 2, low (0): one short paragraph; no introduction naming the writers; no thesis about support; no development; no real conclusion.
Trait 3, about 1: short, choppy sentences with errors (“then” for than, “workers” for workers', missing comma), but the meaning is clear.
Biggest fix: judge the two writers' evidence, with specifics from both passages.

notes.say: Score this out loud the way a trained scorer would, one trait at a time, quoting the response as evidence for each score. The lesson for the student: better grammar would barely help this response. It fails because it is not doing the task.
ask: Would fixing every grammar error make this a strong response? (expected: no; it still argues the issue with no passage evidence)

slides.title: Middle or high?
slides.board:
Response M: “Okafor has evidence from a pilot program. She says jobs were filled faster. She also says the pay gap between men and women was smaller. This shows her argument is good.”

Response H: “Okafor's strongest evidence comes from a six-month pilot with 40 employers. She reports that the average time to fill a job fell ‘from 41 days to 33 days.’ These are measured results, not guesses, so they directly support her claim that posting pay saves time.”

Score each on Trait 1. What changed?
steps: M, about 1: right position and some evidence, but vague (“filled faster,” “smaller”) and the explanation is empty (“This shows her argument is good”).
H, a 2: exact figures with a source (“from 41 days to 33 days,” a 40-employer pilot) and a real reason (“measured results, not guesses”).
What changed: vague → specific; empty explanation → real explanation; a link to her exact claim (saving time).

notes.say: Let the student do the scoring and give reasons before you reveal. Both paragraphs judge the support, so neither is a zero. The difference is specificity and explanation. Have the student name exactly which words in H do the work that M skipped.
ask: Which sentence in M is the empty explanation? (expected: “This shows her argument is good.”)
notes.answer: M earns about 1 on Trait 1 (right idea, vague evidence, empty explanation). H shows what a 2 looks like (specific, accurate, explained, linked).
notes.watch: Students sometimes score M a zero because it is short. Remind them that it does judge the support with real (if vague) evidence, which is middle-level work.

slides.title: Your turn: plan and organize
slides.board:
1. It is minute 32. You have an introduction and one body paragraph. What do you do now?

2. Make this specific with Passage A: “Okafor shows that a lot of employers liked the pilot.”

3. Where does it go (intro, body, conclusion, delete)? (a) “In the end, measured results outweigh one owner's predictions.” (b) “Honestly, I would never work for a business like Whitlock's.”
steps: 1. Write a short second body paragraph on the weaker writer (about 5 min), then a two- or three-sentence conclusion by about minute 38. Skip the optional third paragraph. Revise and edit.
2. Sample: “Okafor reports that when the pilot ended, 37 of the 40 participating employers planned to keep posting pay ranges on their own.”
3. (a) Conclusion; (b) Delete (personal opinion, and it attacks the writer).

notes.say: Start a four-minute timer and stay quiet. When time is up, the student gives each answer with a reason before you reveal anything.
notes.answer: 1. Finish a short body paragraph on the weaker writer, write the conclusion by about minute 38, then revise and edit; drop the optional paragraph. 2. Any accurate version using “37 of the 40” and “keep posting.” 3. (a) Conclusion. (b) Delete.
notes.watch: On problem 2, check the numbers. A student who writes “all 40” or “most employers raised pay” has distorted the evidence.

slides.title: Your turn: revise and edit
slides.board:
1. Fix three errors: “Whitlock say that the pilot employers volunteered, this means there results might not apply to everyone.”

2. Fix three errors: “Okafor's numbers comes from a real pilot, its not a guess.”

3. Which trait is weakest? A response is clean and well organized but never mentions either writer's evidence.
steps: 1. “Whitlock says that the pilot employers volunteered, which means their results might not apply to everyone.” (A period or semicolon before “This means” also fixes the splice.)
2. “Okafor's numbers come from a real pilot; they are not a guess.”
3. Trait 1: no evidence from the passages and no judgment of the support.

notes.say: Three minutes. These are the most common essay errors, so treat them as a rehearsal for the final edit. For problem 3, the student must name the trait and give the reason.
notes.answer: 1. says; comma splice fixed (which / period / semicolon); their. 2. come; comma splice fixed; “its” replaced with “they are” to agree with the plural “numbers.” 3. Trait 1.
notes.watch: In problem 2, students often change “its” to “it's.” That fixes the apostrophe but not the agreement: “numbers … it's” does not match. Push for “they are.”

slides.title: Full RLA review map
slides.board:
Question familyKey move
Informational readingMain idea, inference, structure, purpose: predict, match, prove
Literary readingRead actions, not just words; tone, figurative language, theme
Language (drop-downs)Read the whole sentence with each choice; find the subject
ArgumentsClaim, evidence, red flags: generalization, slippery slope, bandwagon, attack

Traps: too narrow · too broad · not stated · distorted

notes.say: Now we zoom out to the whole RLA test. About three-quarters of the reading is informational and a quarter literary, and roughly a third of the items outside the essay are language items in a drop-down format. The same habits work everywhere: read the question first, predict, match, and prove it with a line from the text. And every argument question is also essay practice, because it uses the same red flags.
ask: What are the four answer traps? (expected: too narrow, too broad, not stated, distorted)
On a drop-down item, what do you do before choosing? (expected: read the whole sentence with each choice)

slides.title: A literary question, start to finish
slides.board:
Grace had swept the church steps every Saturday for eleven years. When the new pastor thanked her at the service, she studied the hymnal in her lap. Afterward she told her sister it was “a lot of fuss over a broom.” That evening she called her son and her cousin and told them the whole story, twice.

What does the passage suggest about Grace?
steps: Says: “a lot of fuss over a broom,” which sounds like she did not care.
Does: looks down during the praise (embarrassed), then calls two relatives and tells the story twice each (proud).
Predict: she is embarrassed by public praise but secretly pleased.
Trap: an answer like “she thinks sweeping is unimportant” takes her words too literally.

notes.say: Model the literary move: compare what a character says with what she does. Predict before looking at choices, then name the trap a careless reader falls into here, which is believing her words.
ask: Which tells you more about Grace, her words or her actions? (expected: her actions)

slides.title: Your turn: full review
slides.board:
1. “Dev said he didn't care about the game, but he checked the score on his phone eleven times during dinner.” What can you infer about Dev?

2. Name the red flag: “If we allow food trucks downtown, soon every restaurant on Main Street will close.”

3. Choose: “Neither the manager nor the cashiers (was / were) told about the change.”

4. Name the trap: the main idea of a whole article about city trees is given as “Trees lower electric bills.”
steps: 1. He cares a lot about the game; his actions contradict his words.
2. Slippery slope: one step leads to disaster, with no evidence.
3. were: with neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, “cashiers” (plural).
4. Too narrow: one detail, not the whole article.

notes.say: Four minutes, one question from each family. Have the student name the skill as well as the answer; that is how they will know what to review this week.
notes.answer: 1. Dev cares about the game (actions over words). 2. Slippery slope. 3. were. 4. Too narrow.
notes.watch: On problem 3, students often choose “was” because “manager” comes first. Teach the rule: with either/or and neither/nor, match the subject closest to the verb.

slides.title: GED question: weak evidence
slides.board:
A learner wants to show that Whitlock's argument (Passage B) is weakly supported. Which detail from his passage would be most effective to critique?

A. “Many business owners I know agree that this rule could tear their teams apart.”
B. “But the 40 employers in that program volunteered, which means they were already comfortable posting pay.”
C. “Every applicant brings different skills and experience to the table.”
D. “I have owned Whitlock Printing on Second Street for nineteen years.”
steps: B is not the best target: it is Whitlock's fairest point. A strong response concedes it and answers it rather than calling it weak.
C is a reasonable general statement; critiquing it would not show much.
D is background that gives him some credibility; it is not a claim to critique.
A is correct: a vague appeal to unnamed people (who? how many?) that readers cannot check. It is weak support and easy to explain.

notes.say: Treat this like the real test. Have the student predict what a weak detail looks like before reading the options: something vague, unsupported, or illogical. Then eliminate one at a time, naming why each wrong choice is not the best target.
ask: Before the options: what makes evidence weak? (expected: vague, one story, unsupported prediction, faulty reasoning)
notes.answer: A. B is his best point (concede and answer it), C is a reasonable statement, D is background.

slides.title: GED question: language drop-down
slides.board:
The Council members, along with the mayor, ______ expected to vote on the ordinance in May.

A. is
B. are
C. was
D. being
steps: A, “is,” is singular; it agrees with “mayor,” which is not the subject.
C, “was,” is singular and past; the vote is in the future, and the subject is plural.
D, “being,” cannot be the main verb; it leaves a fragment.
B is correct: the subject is “members” (plural); “along with the mayor” does not change it.

notes.say: This is the drop-down format the student will see many times. Show the move: find the real subject and set aside the phrase between it and the verb. “Along with the mayor” is extra information, not part of the subject.
ask: What is the subject? (expected: members)
notes.answer: B, are. The subject is “The Council members”; “along with the mayor” is an interrupting phrase.
notes.watch: Students pick “is” because “mayor” sits right next to the blank. Teach them to cover phrases like “along with,” “as well as,” and “together with.”

slides.title: GED question: literary detail
slides.board:
Mr. Alvarez had taught shop for thirty-one years. On his last day, he walked through the empty room, touching each workbench as if checking it for dust. He found none. He had wiped every bench himself that morning.

The detail about touching each workbench mainly suggests that Mr. Alvarez

A. does not trust the custodians to clean the room.
B. is quietly saying goodbye to a place he cares about.
C. is angry that he has been forced to retire.
D. plans to return to teach the class next year.
steps: A is too literal: he wiped the benches himself that morning, so he is not really checking for dust.
C is not stated: nothing suggests anger or being forced out.
D is contradicted: it is his last day.
B is correct: touching each bench in an empty room on his last day after thirty-one years is a quiet goodbye.

notes.say: Predict first: why would someone touch benches he already knows are clean? Then eliminate, naming the trap each time.
ask: If the benches were already clean, why does he touch them? (expected: to say goodbye; it is about feeling, not dust)
notes.answer: B. A is too literal, C is not stated, D is contradicted by “his last day.”

slides.title: GED strategy: the 38-minute alarm
slides.board:
At about 7 minutes left on the essay clock: stop drafting, even mid-paragraph.

  1. Finish the thought in one sentence.
  2. Write a short conclusion if you have none.
  3. Revise (big), then edit (small).

Test day: check the clock after each passage · flag and move on · answer every question (no penalty for guessing) · on the essay, use every minute.

notes.say: Scorers grade what is on the page. A finished, clean response almost always beats a longer one that stops mid-sentence or is full of errors. Make the 38-minute alarm a habit in every practice essay this week. For the rest of the test: pace by passage, flag and return, and never leave a question blank, since a blank earns nothing. The essay has its own time limit, so unused minutes there do not carry over; spend them revising.
ask: What do you do when the clock shows 7 minutes left? (expected: stop drafting, finish the thought, conclusion, then revise and edit)

slides.title: Recap and next steps
slides.board:
• Plan: read 8 · plan 5 · draft 25 · revise and edit 7.
  • Blueprint: intro with thesis → body (both writers) → concession → conclusion.
  • PEEL: specific, accurate evidence, always explained.
  • Revise first, then edit.
  • Traits: 1 argument and evidence · 2 organization · 3 standard English.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice Set A (Set B if under 80%) → Exit Check → a full timed essay this week

notes.say: Have the student recite the 45-minute plan and PEEL from memory before revealing the recap. Then walk through what comes next: the Student Lesson reviews today step by step with checks, Practice Set A has 15 GED-style questions with the reasoning behind every wrong answer, and the Exit Check confirms readiness. This week they should also write one full response to a pair of passages with a 45-minute timer and score it against the three traits.
ask: What is one habit you will use on your next essay? (expected: any specific habit, such as the 38-minute alarm, PEEL, or revising before editing)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
Last week you learned to read two opposing arguments, decide which one is better supported, and write a thesis. This week you turn that plan into a complete Extended Response in 45 minutes, and you review the whole RLA test. You will learn to:

  • follow a 45-minute plan and the blueprint of a strong response
  • build PEEL body paragraphs with specific evidence from both passages
  • revise, then edit, in the last seven minutes
  • score responses with the GED's three traits, using low, middle, and high samples
  • review reading, language, and argument questions from the whole course

Most examples use one pair of passages about the city of Harlow. Passage A, by Denise Okafor, argues that employers with fifteen or more workers should post a pay range in every job ad. Passage B, by business owner Gary Whitlock, argues against it. You will read both in full in Practice; the key facts appear on these screens as you need them.

screens.title: The 45-minute plan
screens.html:
The Extended Response has its own clock: about 45 minutes. The biggest reason strong readers score low is that they run out of time. A plan protects you.

MinutesJob
0–8Read. Prompt first, then both passages. Mark each writer's claim, best evidence, and weak spots.
8–13Plan. Decide which argument is better supported. Write the thesis. List 2–3 body points with evidence.
13–38Draft. Introduction (about 3 min), body paragraphs (about 6–7 min each), conclusion (about 3 min).
38–45Revise, then edit. About 3 minutes on big problems, about 4 on small ones.

If you fall behind, shorten a body paragraph. Never skip the conclusion or the final edit.

check.prompt: In the 45-minute plan, how many minutes are saved at the end for revising and editing? Type the number.
check.hint: Look at the last row of the plan and subtract the start minute from the end minute.
check.explain: The last row of the plan is minutes 38–45: 45 − 38 = 7 minutes, about 3 to revise and about 4 to edit. Students who skip this step lose easy points on Trait 3 and often leave a confusing sentence they could have fixed.

mistakes.why: Five minutes is the planning step (minutes 8 to 13). The revise-and-edit step runs from minute 38 to minute 45.
Twenty-five minutes is the drafting step (minutes 13 to 38). The time saved at the end is 45 − 38.
Eight minutes is the reading step at the start (minutes 0 to 8). Look at the last row of the table.

screens.title: Plan in five minutes: the T-chart
screens.html:
Planning is where you decide what you will prove. Draw a quick T-chart: one column for each writer. Under each, note the claim, the evidence, and anything weak or unfair. Then write your thesis from the chart.

Okafor (A): for posting payWhitlock (B): against
Pilot, 40 employers: 22% fewer applicants who later refused the pay; time to fill a job fell from 41 to 33 daysOne story: the press operator he hired
County review: men's/women's starting-pay gap about half as largePrediction: employees “will demand raises” (no evidence)
Answers critics: under-15 exemption; a range, not an exact salary; 37 of 40 kept postingSlippery slope: city will tell owners “what to pay”; vague “many business owners I know”
Fair point: pilot employers volunteered

Thesis: Okafor's argument is better supported because she relies on measured results and answers her critics, while Whitlock relies on one story and predictions he never supports.

check.prompt: A learner is filling in the Whitlock column of a T-chart. Which note belongs under weak spots in Whitlock's argument?
check.hint: Ask of each note: whose passage is it from, and is it a strength or a weakness?
check.explain: Whitlock's only support for his claim that a posted range “locks both sides in” is the story of one press operator: one hire, at one shop. That is an anecdote, a weak spot. The pilot, the county review, and the under-fifteen exemption all come from Okafor's passage, and they are strengths of her argument. Mixing up whose evidence is whose is a common planning error; label each column clearly.
options: He supports his main claim with one story about a single press operator he hired.
He cites a pilot program in which hiring time fell from 41 days to 33 days.
He cites a county review showing the starting-pay gap was about half as large.
He answers critics by pointing out that businesses under fifteen workers are exempt.
why: The pilot program is Okafor's evidence, and it is a strength. It belongs in her column, not in Whitlock's.
The county review is Okafor's evidence too. Whitlock never cites a study of any kind.
The exemption is part of Okafor's answer to her critics, which is a strength of her argument, not a weakness of Whitlock's.

screens.title: The blueprint of a strong response
screens.html:
Every high-scoring response has the same skeleton:

  • Introduction (2–4 sentences): frame the issue, name both writers and their positions, end with your thesis.
  • Body 1: the stronger writer's best evidence and why it is strong.
  • Body 2: the weaker writer's evidence and why it is weak (one story, a prediction, a vague source, faulty reasoning).
  • Body 3 (if time allows): admit the weaker writer's best point, then explain why it does not change your judgment.
  • Conclusion (2–3 sentences): restate your judgment in new words and sum up the reasons. No new evidence.

Some sentences belong nowhere. A sentence about your own opinion of the issue, or a story from your own life, should be deleted. The task is to judge the support.

check.prompt: Each sentence was written for a response about the Harlow passages. Drag each one to where it belongs, or to Delete if it does not belong in the response at all.
check.hint: Introductions frame the issue, bodies give passage evidence, conclusions sum up. What about a story from the writer's own life?
check.explain: Introduction: “Two writers disagree …” frames the issue. Body: the 37-of-40 sentence gives specific evidence from Passage A. Conclusion: “Taken together …” sums up the judgment. Delete: the sister's story is personal experience. The GED task asks you to judge the passages' evidence, not to add your own.
choices: Two writers disagree about whether Harlow employers should have to post pay ranges in their job ads.
Okafor reports that 37 of the 40 pilot employers planned to keep posting ranges after the pilot ended.
My sister quit a job last year because the pay was lower than the ad suggested.
Taken together, Okafor's data and her answers to critics make hers the better-supported argument.
check.why: The most common mistake is keeping the sister's story in a body paragraph because it seems to support Okafor. It is the writer's own experience, not evidence from the passages, so it should be deleted.

screens.title: Writing the introduction
screens.html:
An introduction does three jobs in two to four sentences. 1. Frame the issue, often as a question. 2. Name both writers and their positions. 3. End with your thesis: which argument is better supported, and a quick preview of why.

Keep evidence out of the introduction; it belongs in the body. Leave out “I think” and “I believe.” Your thesis already states your judgment.

example.prompt: Write an introduction for a response about the Harlow passages.
steps: Frame the issue: “Should employers have to tell job seekers what a job pays before they apply?”
Name both writers: “Denise Okafor, director of the Harlow Workforce Center, supports a city rule requiring pay ranges in job ads, while business owner Gary Whitlock opposes it.”

End with the thesis: “Okafor's argument is better supported because she backs her claims with results from a real pilot and answers her critics, while Whitlock relies on one story and predictions he never supports.”
example.answer: Three sentences: issue, writers, thesis. No evidence yet, no personal opinion, and the last sentence tells the reader exactly what the body paragraphs will prove.

check.prompt: A learner has written the first two sentences of an introduction about the Harlow passages: the issue and the two writers' positions. Which sentence should come next, to end the introduction?
check.hint: Which sentence states a judgment about the two arguments, and previews the reasons for it?
check.explain: The last sentence of an introduction is the thesis. “Okafor's argument is better supported because she uses measured results and answers her critics, while Whitlock relies on one story” states the judgment and previews the reasons. The 41-to-33-day sentence is tempting because it is specific and accurate, but it is evidence, and evidence goes in the body.
options: Okafor's argument is better supported because she uses measured results and answers her critics, while Whitlock relies on one story.
Okafor reports that during the pilot, the average time to fill an open job fell all the way from 41 days down to 33 days.
I have always believed that a person's pay should be private, so I personally lean toward Whitlock's side of this debate.
In this essay, I am going to tell you about the two articles and what each of the two writers thinks about pay ranges.
why: This is strong, specific evidence, but evidence belongs in a body paragraph. The introduction should end with the thesis that the evidence will prove.
This gives the writer's personal belief about the issue. The task is to judge which argument is better supported, not which side you lean toward.
This only announces the topic. An introduction should end with a thesis that makes a judgment.

screens.title: PEEL body paragraphs
screens.html:
Every body paragraph follows the same four steps:

  1. Point: a topic sentence that makes one claim about the quality of a writer's support.
  2. Evidence: a short, exact quotation or a precise paraphrase, with the writer's name (“Okafor reports …”).
  3. Explain: one or two sentences on why this evidence is strong or weak. This is where most of the score lives.
  4. Link: tie it back to your thesis.

Quoting without explaining scores like a summary. Every piece of evidence needs a “because” or “this shows” sentence after it.

check.prompt:
Label each sentence of this body paragraph with its PEEL step.

(1) Whitlock's argument rests on much weaker support than Okafor's. {{0}}

(2) To show that a posted range “locks both sides in,” he describes hiring a single press operator. {{1}}

(3) One hire at one shop cannot show what will happen across an entire city, so this story proves very little. {{2}}

(4) Because his main claim rests on a single anecdote, Whitlock's position is the less convincing of the two. {{3}}
check.hint: The Point makes a claim, the Evidence comes from the passage, the Explain says why, and the Link ties back to the thesis.
check.explain: (1) Point: the claim about the quality of Whitlock's support. (2) Evidence: a short, exact quotation and what Whitlock offers. (3) Explain: why one hire is weak evidence. (4) Link: ties the paragraph back to the thesis that Whitlock's position is less convincing.

options: Point
Evidence
Explain
Link
why: Sentence 1 cites nothing from the passage. It states the paragraph's claim, which is the Point.
Sentence 1 does not explain any evidence yet; no evidence has appeared. It is the topic sentence, the Point.
Sentence 1 opens the paragraph and states its claim. A Link comes at the end and ties back to the thesis.

options: Point
Evidence
Explain
Link
why: The Point was sentence 1. Sentence 2 quotes Whitlock and describes what he offers as support, which is Evidence.
Sentence 2 reports what Whitlock wrote but does not yet judge it. The judging comes in sentence 3.
Sentence 2 does not tie back to the thesis; it presents Whitlock's evidence.

options: Point
Evidence
Explain
Link
why: Sentence 3 is not the paragraph's main claim; it explains why the evidence in sentence 2 is weak.
Sentence 3 adds no new evidence from the passage. It judges the evidence already given.
Sentence 3 explains one piece of evidence. The Link is the sentence that ties the paragraph back to the overall judgment.

options: Point
Evidence
Explain
Link
why: Sentence 4 does not open the paragraph. It closes it by tying back to the thesis.
Sentence 4 cites nothing new from the passage.
Sentence 4 does more than explain the story; it connects the paragraph to the thesis about which position is more convincing.

screens.title: Specific, accurate evidence
screens.html:
Specific evidence names the writer and uses the passage's own numbers or words. Accurate evidence matches the passage exactly. A wrong number is worse than no number: it tells the reader you did not check.

Vague (weak)Specific (strong)
Okafor has a lot of facts.Okafor reports that the average time to fill a job fell from 41 days to 33 days during the pilot.
Whitlock says bad things will happen.Whitlock predicts that employees “will demand raises,” but he gives no numbers or examples.

Use attribution verbs to show whose idea it is: reports, argues, cites, predicts, claims. “Claims” is useful for weak evidence: “Whitlock claims that many owners agree.” Quote short phrases exactly, and double-check every number against the passage.

example.prompt: Make this sentence specific: “Okafor shows that pay ranges are fair. She has good evidence about this.”
steps: Ask: which evidence? Find it. Paragraph 3 of Passage A describes a review of hiring records by the Marsh County Labor Office.
Use the passage's own finding: the gap between men's and women's starting pay was about half as large at employers that posted ranges.
Add the Explain step: say why this evidence is strong.
example.answer: “Okafor cites a review of hiring records by the Marsh County Labor Office, which found that the gap between men's and women's starting pay was about half as large at employers that posted ranges. Because this finding comes from actual records rather than opinions, it gives readers solid reason to accept her claim.”

check.prompt: Passage A says: “In fact, when the pilot ended, 37 of the 40 participating employers said they planned to keep posting ranges on their own.” Which sentence uses this evidence specifically and accurately?
check.hint: Compare each choice with the quotation word by word. Check the number and the action.
check.explain: The accurate, specific version keeps the exact number (37 of the 40) and the exact action (planned to keep posting ranges), and it credits Okafor. The other choices are either vague (“a lot … really liked”) or distorted: one changes 37 to all 40, and one changes “posting ranges” into “raised their starting pay.”
options: Okafor reports that 37 of the 40 pilot employers planned to keep posting ranges after the pilot ended.
Okafor reports that all 40 of the pilot employers planned to keep posting pay ranges after the pilot ended.
Okafor reports that 37 of the 40 pilot employers raised their starting pay after the pilot program ended.
Okafor shows that a lot of the employers really liked the pilot program and wanted to keep doing it.
why: This changes the number. The passage says 37 of the 40, not all 40. Misquoting a number tells the reader you did not check the passage.
This changes the meaning. The employers planned to keep posting ranges; the passage never says they raised pay.
This is vague. “A lot” and “really liked” replace the passage's exact number and exact action.

screens.title: Using both passages: concede and answer
screens.html:
The prompt says to analyze both positions. That means you discuss the weaker writer's evidence too, and the strongest responses also admit the weaker writer's best point. This is called a concession. A concession does not switch sides. It shows the reader you weighed everything, and then you answer it.

Pattern: To be fair, [weaker writer] raises one reasonable point: … However, … In the answer, say why the point does not outweigh the other side's evidence: it is unsupported, it is answered by the other writer, or it is small compared with the evidence against it.

example.prompt: Whitlock's best point: the 40 pilot employers volunteered, so their results might not match those of businesses forced to post pay. Write a concession and answer.
steps: Concede: “To be fair, Whitlock raises one reasonable point: the pilot employers volunteered, so their results might not match those of employers who are required to post pay.”
Answer, part 1: point out what is missing. “However, he offers no evidence that the results would be different.”
Answer, part 2: use the other passage. “Okafor also shows that the ordinance was written with small businesses in mind: it exempts those with fewer than fifteen workers and requires only a range.”
example.answer: The paragraph admits the fair point, then shows why it does not change the judgment. The thesis still stands.

check.prompt: Which sentence pair best concedes Whitlock's point about volunteer employers and answers it?
check.hint: A good concession admits the point and then answers it. Which pair keeps the thesis standing?
check.explain: A concession admits the weaker writer's best point (“To be fair, the pilot employers volunteered…”), and an answer explains why it does not change the judgment (“However, Whitlock offers no evidence that the results would differ”). The pair that ends with “Therefore, Whitlock's argument is better supported” is the most tempting wrong answer: it concedes, but then abandons the thesis.
options: To be fair, the pilot employers volunteered, so their results may not apply to all businesses. However, Whitlock offers no evidence that the results would differ.
To be fair, the pilot employers volunteered, so their results may not apply to all businesses. Therefore, Whitlock's argument is better supported than Okafor's.
Whitlock says the pilot employers volunteered. This is a personal attack on Okafor, so readers should ignore the point and focus only on her evidence.
The pilot employers volunteered, which shows they were good companies. That proves the ordinance will work for every business in the whole city.
why: This concedes the point but then switches sides. One fair point does not outweigh Okafor's measured results; a concession should be answered, not surrendered to.
This mislabels the point. Questioning who volunteered is a criticism of the evidence, not an attack on Okafor, and the sentence never really answers it.
This misreads the point and overstates the evidence. Nothing in either passage proves the rule will work for every business.

screens.title: Writing the conclusion
screens.html:
A conclusion is short, two or three sentences, and it is never skipped. It should:

  • restate your judgment in new words (not a copy of the thesis), and
  • sum up the main reasons from both sides.

A conclusion should not add new evidence, switch positions, tell readers to “decide for themselves,” or give your personal opinion on the issue.

Start the conclusion by minute 35 or so, no matter what. A complete response with a short conclusion scores better than an unfinished one.

check.prompt: Which two sentences would work well in the conclusion of a response about the Harlow passages? Select two.
check.hint: A conclusion restates and sums up. Which choices add something new, back away, or attack the writer?
check.explain: The restated judgment (“In the end, Okafor's position is the better supported of the two”) and the summary of reasons from both sides make a complete conclusion. The 37-of-40 sentence is tempting because it is accurate and specific, but it is new evidence. “Decide for themselves,” the personal opinion, and the attack on Whitlock all weaken a conclusion.
options: In the end, Okafor's position is the better supported of the two.
She relies on measured results and answers her critics, while Whitlock depends on one story and guesses.
Okafor also reports that 37 of the 40 pilot employers planned to keep posting ranges on their own.
In the end, readers should study both articles and decide for themselves which writer is right.
Personally, I think every employer in the country should post pay in its job ads.
Whitlock is just a business owner who wants to keep his workers' pay low.
why: This is new evidence. If a detail matters, it belongs in a body paragraph; a conclusion only sums up.
This gives up your judgment. The whole response exists to say which argument is better supported.
This is personal opinion on the issue, which the task does not ask for.
This attacks Whitlock as a person instead of judging his evidence, and Passage B never says anything about the pay he offers.

screens.title: The last seven minutes: revise, then edit
screens.html:
Use the last seven minutes in this order:

1. Revise (big things, about 3 minutes). Is the thesis clear, and does it judge the support? Does each body paragraph start with a point that backs the thesis? Did I explain every piece of evidence? Is there any sentence about my own opinion or life? Delete it.

2. Edit (small things, about 4 minutes). Fragments, run-ons, and comma splices; subject-verb agreement; confused words (their/there/they're, its/it's, then/than, to/too, a lot); capital letters for names; exact quotations and numbers.

Revise before you edit. Fixing commas in a sentence you later delete wastes time, and big problems cost more points.

check.prompt: Sort each fix: is it revising (ideas and organization) or editing (grammar, usage, and mechanics)?
check.hint: Ask: does this fix change the ideas, or only the correctness of the words?
check.explain: Revising changes what the response says and how it is organized: a clearer point, deleting off-task personal material, adding an explanation. Editing fixes the surface: the possessive their, the comma with a coordinating conjunction, and the capital letters in a proper name. Do the revising first.
choices: Replace a vague topic sentence with a clear point about the support
Delete a sentence about your own job search
Add a sentence explaining why a quotation is strong evidence
Change “there results” to “their results”
Add a comma before “but” where it joins two complete sentences
Capitalize “city council” in “the Harlow city council”
check.why: The most common mistake is calling the added explanation sentence an edit because it is only one sentence. Adding an explanation changes the ideas in the paragraph, so it is revising.

screens.title: Your edit checklist
screens.html:
The response box has no spell check, so your eyes are the only checker. Read each sentence once, slowly, looking for these:

ErrorWrongRight
Comma spliceHe gives no data, it is a guess.He gives no data; it is a guess.
AgreementThese numbers supports her claim.These numbers support her claim.
Confused wordsthere results / its a guess / thentheir results / it's a guess / than
Capitalsthe harlow city councilthe Harlow City Council

Then vs. than: then is about time (“first plan, then draft”). Than compares (“stronger than”).

check.prompt: Type the word that correctly fills the blank: “Okafor's evidence is much stronger      Whitlock's.”
check.hint: Is the sentence about time, or is it comparing two things?
check.explain: The sentence compares Okafor's evidence with Whitlock's, so it needs the comparison word than. “Then” is about time. This is one of the most common errors on GED essays and editing items.

mistakes.why: “Then” is about time or order (“first plan, then draft”). This sentence compares two things, so it needs “than.”
“Stronger that Whitlock's” is not standard English. After a comparison word like “stronger,” use “than.”

screens.title: The three scoring traits
screens.html:
Trained scorers read your response and give it 0, 1, or 2 points on each of three traits.

TraitWhat scorers look for
1. Arguments and use of evidenceA clear position on which argument is better supported; specific, relevant evidence from both passages; explanation of why evidence is strong or weak
2. Development and organizationIntroduction, body, conclusion; ideas developed, not just listed; logical order; transitions; a formal, appropriate tone
3. Clarity and standard EnglishClear, varied sentences; correct grammar, usage, capitalization, and punctuation

Scorers know you wrote in 45 minutes, so a few minor errors that do not get in the way of meaning will not cost you a top Trait 3 score. A response that argues only your own opinion, or that copies the passages without analysis, scores low on Trait 1 no matter how well it is written.

check.prompt:
Match each problem to the trait it hurts most.

A response has no introduction or conclusion, and its ideas are listed with no transitions. {{0}}

A response argues that pay ranges are a good idea and never mentions either writer's evidence. {{1}}

A response has comma splices and confused words (there/their) in almost every sentence. {{2}}
check.hint: Trait 1 = what you argue and prove. Trait 2 = how it is built. Trait 3 = how correctly it is written.
check.explain: No introduction or conclusion, no transitions: Trait 2 (organization). Arguing the issue with no passage evidence: Trait 1 (arguments and evidence). Comma splices and confused words throughout: Trait 3 (standard English).

options: Trait 1
Trait 2
Trait 3
why: Trait 1 is about the argument and evidence. Missing paragraphs and transitions are problems of structure, which is Trait 2.
Trait 3 is about sentence-level correctness. A missing introduction is a structure problem, Trait 2.

options: Trait 1
Trait 2
Trait 3
why: The problem is not organization; it is that the response argues the issue and uses no evidence from the passages. That is Trait 1.
Nothing here is a grammar problem. Arguing the issue with no passage evidence hurts Trait 1.

options: Trait 1
Trait 2
Trait 3
why: Comma splices and confused words are about correctness of language, not the argument. That is Trait 3.
The structure might be fine. Sentence-level errors are Trait 3.

screens.title: Scoring a low response
screens.html:
Look at the sample below the way a scorer would. Read it once, then go trait by trait. Ask: Does it judge the support with passage evidence? Is it built with an introduction, body, and conclusion? Is it clearly and correctly written?

A low response usually fails Trait 1 first: it argues the issue, tells a personal story, or attacks a writer instead of judging the evidence.

example.prompt:
Sample response (low):

I think pay ranges are a good idea. When I was looking for work I applied to a warehouse job and it paid way less then I needed. Okafor is right about that. Whitlock just wants to keep his workers pay low. Businesses should be honest. So the city should pass it.
steps: Trait 1 (low, 0): it argues the issue (“pay ranges are a good idea”), uses a personal story as support, and cites nothing specific from either passage. “Whitlock just wants to keep his workers pay low” attacks the writer; Passage B never says that.
Trait 2 (low, 0): one short paragraph, no introduction naming the writers, no thesis about support, no development, no real conclusion.
Trait 3 (low to middle, about 1): the sentences are short and choppy, with errors (“then” for than, “workers” for workers', a missing comma after “work”), but the meaning is still clear.
example.answer: This response would score at the very bottom on Traits 1 and 2. Better grammar alone would not help much; the writer must judge the evidence.

check.prompt: What is the main reason the sample response scores so low on Trait 1?
check.hint: Trait 1 is about the argument and the evidence. What is this response arguing, and what does it use for support?
check.explain: Trait 1 asks whether the response takes a position on which argument is better supported and backs it with specific passage evidence. This response argues the issue, supports it with the writer's own job search, and never examines anything either writer offers. The grammar and structure problems are real, but they belong to Traits 3 and 2.
options: It argues that pay ranges are good using a personal story, and never judges either writer's evidence.
It has several grammar and punctuation errors, such as “then” in place of the word “than.”
It is written as a single paragraph instead of an introduction, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.
It has only one paragraph, and Trait 1 gives no points to a response shorter than five paragraphs.
why: The errors are real, but they belong to Trait 3. Trait 1 is about the argument and the evidence.
The single paragraph is a Trait 2 problem. Trait 1 is about what the response argues and proves.
There is no paragraph minimum for Trait 1. Length alone does not earn Trait 1 points; scorers look at what the response argues and how it uses evidence.

screens.title: From middle to high
screens.html:
A middle response usually has the right idea but thin support. It takes a position on which argument is better supported and mentions evidence from both passages, but the evidence is vague (“jobs were filled faster”) and the explanation is a single empty line (“This shows her argument is good”).

A high response does the same job with specific evidence, a real explanation of why each piece is strong or weak, a concession, clear paragraphs with transitions, and clean sentences. Compare one body paragraph from each in the example.

example.prompt:
Middle:

Okafor has evidence from a pilot program. She says jobs were filled faster. She also says the pay gap between men and women was smaller. This shows her argument is good.

High:

Okafor's strongest evidence comes from the Workforce Center's six-month pilot with 40 employers. She reports that the average time to fill a job fell “from 41 days to 33 days” and adds a county review finding that the gap between men's and women's starting pay was about half as large at employers that posted ranges. These are measured results from real records, not guesses, so they give readers solid reason to accept her claim that posting pay makes hiring faster and fairer.
steps: Specific: “filled faster” becomes “from 41 days to 33 days”; “pay gap was smaller” becomes “about half as large,” credited to a county review.
Explained: “This shows her argument is good” becomes a reason: measured results from real records, not guesses.
Linked: the last sentence ties the evidence to Okafor's exact claim (faster and fairer hiring).
example.answer: The middle paragraph would likely earn about 1 on Trait 1; the high paragraph is what a 2 looks like: specific, accurate, explained, and linked.

check.prompt: Which two changes did the most to move the middle paragraph up to the high one? Select two.
check.hint: Compare the two paragraphs sentence by sentence. What did the writer add?
check.explain: The two biggest changes are specific evidence (exact figures and a named source in place of “filled faster”) and a real explanation of why that evidence is strong. Those are the heart of Trait 1. Adding “I believe,” shortening sentences, or adding a personal story would all make the paragraph weaker.
options: Replacing “jobs were filled faster” with the exact figures, 41 days to 33 days
Explaining why the evidence is strong: measured results from real records, not guesses
Adding “I believe” before the topic sentence so the paragraph sounds more confident
Making the sentences shorter so that the paragraph is quicker to read
Adding a personal story about a job that paid less than the ad suggested
why: The high paragraph does not use “I believe.” Personal-opinion phrases weaken an evaluation; the evidence should carry the confidence.
The high paragraph actually uses longer, more developed sentences. Shortness was part of the middle paragraph's problem.
Neither paragraph uses a personal story, and adding one would move the response off task.

screens.title: Full review: reading questions
screens.html:
About three-quarters of RLA reading is informational (articles, letters, workplace documents, arguments) and about a quarter is literary (fiction you have not seen before). The same habits work on both: read the question first, predict the answer in your own words, match it to a choice, and prove it with a line from the text.

Wrong answers fall into four traps: too narrow, too broad, not stated, and distorted. In literary passages, watch for one more: taking a character's words too literally. Characters often say one thing and show another through their actions.

check.prompt:
Grace had swept the front steps of the church every Saturday for eleven years. When the new pastor thanked her at the service, the whole room turned to look, and she studied the hymnal in her lap as if it held the answer to a hard question. Afterward, in the parking lot, she told her sister it was “a lot of fuss over a broom.” But that evening she called her son in Atlanta, and then her cousin in Tampa, and told them both the whole story, twice.

What does the passage suggest about Grace?
check.hint: Compare what Grace says with what she does that evening. Which tells you more?
check.explain: Two clues point one way: during the praise she stares at the hymnal (embarrassment), and afterward she plays it down (“a lot of fuss over a broom”). But that evening she calls two relatives and tells them “the whole story, twice.” Her actions show she is proud and pleased. The “unimportant work” choice is the trap: it believes her words instead of her actions.
options: She is embarrassed by public praise but is quietly very pleased by it.
She is annoyed with the pastor for embarrassing her and plans to quit.
She believes sweeping the steps is unimportant work that needs no thanks.
She is upset with her sister and refuses to talk about the church service.
why: This is not stated. Nothing in the passage says she is annoyed or plans to stop; her phone calls suggest she is pleased.
This takes her words too literally. She calls it “a lot of fuss,” but then she tells the story to two relatives, twice each.
This is not supported. She does talk to her sister about the service, in the parking lot.

screens.title: Full review: language questions
screens.html:
About a third of the RLA test outside the essay checks language: drop-down menus inside a letter, memo, or article, where you choose the correct word or punctuation. Read the whole sentence with each choice before you decide. The most-tested errors are the same ones on your edit checklist:

  • subject-verb agreement, especially when words come between the subject and the verb (“Each of the workers has”)
  • pronouns that match their nouns
  • comma splices, run-ons, and fragments
  • transitions that show the right relationship (contrast, cause, example)
  • confused words and capitalization

check.prompt: Click the sentence in this memo that contains an error in standard English.
check.hint: Find the subject of each verb. Ignore any phrase that starts with “of” between the subject and the verb.
check.explain: Set aside the words between the subject and the verb: “Each (of the workers on the crew) have been asked.” The subject is Each, which means one at a time and is singular, so the verb must be has: “Each of the workers on the crew has been asked…” The other sentences are correct.
spans: Starting Monday, the employee parking lot will be repaved.
During the work, staff should park in the lot behind the library.
The repaving is expected to take three days, weather permitting.
Each of the workers on the crew have been asked to keep one lane open for deliveries.
Thank you for your patience while the lot is improved.
check.why: The most common miss is reading “workers … have” and hearing nothing wrong. The subject is “Each,” which is singular; “of the workers on the crew” only describes it. The verb must be “has.”

screens.title: Full review: evaluating arguments
screens.html:
Argument questions ask you to find a writer's claim, judge the evidence, and spot faulty reasoning. Five red flags appear again and again:

Red flagWhat it looks like
Hasty generalizationOne case turned into a rule
Slippery slopeOne step will lead to disaster, with no proof
Bandwagon“Everyone agrees,” so it must be right
Personal attackAttacking the person instead of the evidence
Vague source“Studies show” or “people I know” with no details

These are the same weaknesses you name in your Extended Response, so every argument question is also essay practice.

check.prompt: A letter to the editor says: “Our town should not build a skate park. My nephew broke his wrist skateboarding last year, which proves that skate parks are too dangerous.” Which flaw does this reasoning show?
check.hint: How many examples does the writer give, and how big is the conclusion drawn from them?
check.explain: One injury, which did not even happen at a skate park as far as the letter says, is used to “prove” that all skate parks are too dangerous. Drawing a broad rule from a single case is a hasty generalization. To be convincing, the writer would need injury rates or data from skate parks.
options: A hasty generalization: it turns one person's injury into a rule about all skate parks
A slippery slope: it claims one step will lead to a chain of worse and worse results
A bandwagon appeal: it says the claim is true because most people already believe it
A personal attack: it criticizes the people who support the park instead of their ideas
why: The letter predicts no chain of events. It jumps from one injury to a conclusion about all skate parks.
The letter never mentions what most people believe. Its only support is one nephew's injury.
The letter does not mention the park's supporters at all, so it is not attacking anyone.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
Here is what to carry into Practice and onto test day:

  • 45-minute plan: read and mark (about 8), plan and thesis (about 5), draft (about 25), revise and edit (about 7).
  • Blueprint: introduction ending in a thesis; body paragraphs on each writer's evidence; an optional concession paragraph; a short conclusion with no new evidence.
  • PEEL: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link. The explanation earns the points.
  • Specific and accurate: name the writer, use exact numbers and words, check them.
  • Revise, then edit. Big problems first, then splices, agreement, confused words, capitals.
  • Three traits: 1 argument and evidence, 2 organization, 3 standard English, each 0–2.
  • Full review: predict, match, prove; name the trap; read the whole sentence on language items; name the red flag on argument items.
  • Judge the support, not the issue. Leave your own opinion out.

Next: Practice Set A (15 questions). Score 80% or higher on first tries to master it; otherwise take Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

stimuli.title: Passage A: Post the Pay: Every Job Ad Should List a Salary Range
stimuli.html:
(1) Every week at the Harlow Workforce Center, I meet job seekers who have spent hours filling out applications, taking skills tests, and arranging child care for interviews, only to learn at the very end that the job pays far less than they can live on. That waste of time and effort is avoidable. The Harlow City Council should pass the proposed ordinance requiring every employer with fifteen or more workers to include a good-faith pay range in each job posting.

(2) Posted pay ranges save time for employers and applicants alike. Last year, the Workforce Center ran a six-month pilot program in which 40 local employers agreed to list pay ranges in their job ads. According to the center's final report, those employers received 22 percent fewer applications from people who later turned down an offer because the pay was too low. The average time it took them to fill an open position also fell, from 41 days to 33 days. Hiring managers told us they spent fewer hours interviewing candidates who were never going to accept.

(3) Pay ranges also make hiring fairer. When pay is kept secret, the workers who know the most about salaries, or who feel most comfortable negotiating, tend to get the best offers. Everyone else is left guessing. A review of hiring records by the Marsh County Labor Office found that among workers hired into the same job titles, the gap between men's and women's starting pay was about half as large at employers that posted ranges as at employers that did not.

(4) Some business owners worry that posting pay will expose private information or burden small shops. The ordinance was written with those concerns in mind. It does not apply to businesses with fewer than fifteen employees, and it requires a range, not an exact salary, so employers still have room to pay more for experience. In fact, when the pilot ended, 37 of the 40 participating employers said they planned to keep posting ranges on their own.

(5) Job seekers deserve to know what a job pays before they invest their time in applying. Employers deserve applicants who are ready to say yes. One line in every job ad serves both. The Council should pass the ordinance.
stimuli.source: By Denise Okafor, director of the Harlow Workforce Center (original passage written for KCE GED Prep)

stimuli.title: Passage B: Keep the City Out of Our Job Ads
stimuli.html:
(1) I have owned Whitlock Printing on Second Street for nineteen years. In that time I have hired dozens of people, and I have never once had trouble talking about pay with an applicant. Now the Harlow City Council wants to tell me how to write my own help-wanted ads. The proposed pay-range ordinance is a bad idea that will hurt the very businesses that keep this city working.

(2) Pay should be a conversation, not a number printed in advance. Every applicant brings different skills and experience to the table. Last spring, I hired a press operator who turned out to have ten years of experience I had not expected, so I paid her well above what I had planned. If I had posted a range, she might have looked at the top number, decided it was too low, and never applied at all. A posted range locks both sides in before they have even met.

(3) The ordinance will also cause trouble inside workplaces. When current employees see a posting with a range higher than what they earn, they will demand raises, and owners who cannot afford them will lose good people. Many business owners I know agree that this rule could tear their teams apart. And once the city controls our job ads, it will not be long before it starts telling us what to pay.

(4) Supporters like to point to the Workforce Center's pilot program. But the 40 employers in that program volunteered, which means they were already comfortable posting pay. Of course it worked for them. Their experience tells us nothing about what will happen when every business is forced to follow the rule, whether it wants to or not.

(5) Harlow's employers are not the enemy. We take the risks, we meet the payroll, and we create the jobs this city depends on. The Council should trust us to treat our workers fairly and vote no on this ordinance.
stimuli.source: By Gary Whitlock, owner of Whitlock Printing and member of the Harlow Small Business Alliance (original passage written for KCE GED Prep)

stimuli.title: Draft Response: Which Argument Is Better Supported?
stimuli.html:
A GED learner wrote this response to Passages A and B in 45 minutes. It has not yet been revised or edited. Blanks (A) through (E) mark places to be edited.

(1) Should employers in Harlow be required to list pay ranges in their job ads? Denise Okafor, director of the Harlow Workforce Center, argues that they should, while print shop owner Gary Whitlock argues that the city should stay out of hiring. Okafor's argument is better supported because she relies on measured results and answers her opponents' concerns, while Whitlock relies mostly on one personal story and predictions he does not back up.

(2) Okafor's evidence comes from a real test, not a guess. (A) the employers in her pilot program posted pay ranges, they received 22 percent fewer applications from people who would reject the pay and filled jobs faster, with the average time to fill a position dropping from 41 days to 33 days.
