Personally, I think every job ad should list the pay, because I hate wasting time on applications. Okafor also cites a county review showing that the pay gap between men and women hired into the same jobs was about half as large at employers that posted ranges. These numbers (B) her claim that pay ranges make hiring both faster and fairer.

(3) Whitlock's argument is weaker. He describes hiring a press operator who had more experience than he expected, but one story about one hire cannot show what will happen across a whole city. He also predicts that the ordinance will lead the city to control (C) no evidence for this prediction. To be fair, Whitlock makes one strong point: the employers in the pilot volunteered, so (D) results may not apply to every business. Even so, one reasonable doubt does not outweigh Okafor's data, and Whitlock offers no numbers of his own.

(4) In conclusion, both writers care about Harlow's workers and businesses, but Okafor makes the stronger case. The (E) should look closely at the evidence each writer provides. That is my opinion about the two articles.

stimuli.title: Closing Time
stimuli.source: Original short story written for KCE GED Prep
stimuli.html:
(1) At 9:40 every night, Marisol turned the sign on the Lakeview Diner from OPEN to CLOSED and began the work nobody saw. She stacked the chairs on the tables, legs in the air like a field of overturned beetles, and ran the mop in long, even strokes the way her father had taught her when the diner was still his.

(2) Her son, Teo, sat at the counter with a geometry book he had not opened. “You don't have to stay,” she told him. “Take the bus.”

(3) “The last bus left at nine-fifteen,” he said, without looking up from his phone.

(4) She knew that. She had known it when she asked. She pushed the mop under the booth where her father used to sit with his coffee and the newspaper, reading the prices of things out loud as if the numbers were news from a distant country. Eggs, up again. Flour, up again. He had kept every receipt in a shoebox, and she still had the shoebox, though she had stopped opening it.

(5) “Mom.” Teo had turned the phone face down. “Mr. Okoye says if I pass the next test, I can move up to the advanced class.”

(6) The mop stopped. She looked at the book, still closed, and then at her son, who was suddenly very interested in a salt shaker.

(7) “Then open the book,” she said.

(8) He did. She went back to the floor, slower now, working around the stool where he sat so she would not have to ask him to move. After a while she heard the scratch of his pencil, steady as rain on the awning, and she found she was mopping the same clean square twice just to keep listening.

(9) At 10:30 she turned off every light but the one above the counter.

stimuli.title: Passage A: Ride Free: Eastvale Should Drop Bus Fares
stimuli.source: By Lena Fortier, chair of the Eastvale Transit Riders Council (original passage written for KCE GED Prep)
stimuli.html:
(1) Every morning at the Route 4 stop on Mill Street, I watch riders dig through their pockets for exact change while the bus idles and the schedule slips. Many of them are headed to jobs that pay by the hour, and some have already decided which errands to skip this week to cover bus fare. Eastvale can fix both problems at once. The City Council should make all city buses fare-free starting next July.

(2) Free fares bring more riders onto the bus. From March through August of last year, the city ran a fare-free trial on Route 4, its busiest line. According to the Eastvale Transit Department's report on the trial, weekday ridership on Route 4 rose 31 percent compared with the same months the year before, while ridership on the city's other routes, which still charged fares, rose 2 percent. A rider survey taken during the trial found that 38 percent of new riders had previously driven alone to work or school.

(3) Free fares also make buses faster. When no one has to pay at the door, riders board through every door at once. During the trial, the average time a Route 4 bus spent at each stop fell from 18 seconds to 11 seconds, and the share of Route 4 trips that arrived on time rose from 71 percent to 84 percent.

(4) Critics ask how the city would pay for free buses. The answer is that fares cover less than people think. Last year, fares brought in $1.2 million, about 9 percent of the bus system's budget, and the city spent $380,000 of that amount just to collect them: fareboxes, repairs, armored-car pickups, and counting the cash. The real cost to the city would therefore be about $820,000 a year. The Transit Department has proposed covering that gap with revenue from the new downtown parking meters, which are expected to bring in $1.1 million a year. No new tax is required.

(5) A bus fare is a small charge that keeps people off the bus and slows down everyone who is already on it. The trial showed what happens when Eastvale removes it. The Council should vote yes.

stimuli.title: Passage B: Free Buses Are Not Free
stimuli.source: By Doug Parrish, owner of Parrish Hardware (original passage written for KCE GED Prep)
stimuli.html:
(1) I have run Parrish Hardware on Mill Street for twenty-two years, and the Route 4 bus stops right outside my door. I want buses that work for this city. But the plan to stop charging fares is a feel-good idea that Eastvale cannot afford, and the people pushing it have not thought it through.

(2) Free service changes who rides and how they behave. One afternoon last summer, during the fare-free trial, I watched a man ride Route 4 from one end of the line to the other three times, just to stay out of the heat. If a bus becomes a free place to sit all day, regular riders will stop feeling safe, and they will go back to their cars.

(3) The money will not stop at the parking meters, either. The meters were sold to downtown businesses as a way to pay for street repairs, and now the bus system wants that money too. Once riders get used to paying nothing, they will expect free buses forever, and the only way to keep paying for them will be to raise property taxes on every homeowner in Eastvale. Everyone I talk to on Mill Street says the same thing: this plan is a disaster waiting to happen.

(4) Supporters point proudly to last year's trial. But the trial ran only from March through August, when school was out for part of the time, the weather was mild, and the newness of a free bus drew curious riders who will not keep riding once the excitement wears off. Six warm months on one route cannot tell us what a full year on every route will look like.

(5) Eastvale's buses need better shelters, newer vehicles, and more frequent service. Those things cost money, and fares help pay for them. The Council should keep the fares and spend its energy fixing the buses we have.

stimuli.title: Draft Response: Which Argument Is Better Supported?
stimuli.html:
A GED learner wrote this response to Passages A and B (Eastvale bus fares) in 45 minutes. It has not yet been revised or edited. Blanks (A) through (E) mark places to be edited.

(1) Should Eastvale stop charging fares on city buses? Lena Fortier, who chairs the Eastvale Transit Riders Council, argues that it should, while hardware store owner Doug Parrish argues that the city cannot afford free buses. Fortier's argument is better supported because she relies on measured results from a real trial and explains how the city would cover the cost, while Parrish relies mostly on one story and predictions he never backs up.

(2) Fortier's evidence comes from a real trial, not a guess. (A) weekday ridership on Route 4 rose 31 percent during the fare-free months, ridership on the routes that still charged fares rose only 2 percent. My cousin rides the bus every day, and she says free fares would save her a lot of money. Fortier also reports that the average time a bus spent at each stop fell from 18 seconds to 11 seconds. These results (B) her claim that free fares bring in riders and speed up service.

(3) Parrish's argument is weaker. He describes one man who rode the bus to stay out of the heat, but one rider on one afternoon cannot show how thousands of riders will behave. He also predicts that free buses will force the city to raise property (C) offers no evidence for this prediction. To be fair, Parrish makes one reasonable point: the trial lasted only six warm months on one route, so (D) results might not hold for a full year. Even so, Parrish gives no numbers of his own, and Fortier's comparison with the other routes shows that the jump in riders was not just a summer pattern.

(4) In conclusion, both writers want Eastvale's buses to work well, but Fortier makes the stronger case. The (E) should weigh the evidence carefully before it votes. That is just what I think about it.

stimuli.title: The Spare Key
stimuli.source: Original short story written for KCE GED Prep
stimuli.html:
(1) The morning of her road test, Kiara found her grandfather already in the driveway, wiping down the hood of his old blue sedan with a towel that had once been a shirt.

(2) “It's going to rain,” she said. “You're just going to get it wet again.”

(3) “Examiners notice a clean car,” Grandpa Lewis said, and kept wiping.

(4) He had taught her to drive in that car, three Sundays in a row in the empty lot behind the church, with his right hand hovering an inch above the emergency brake the whole time. He never said he was nervous. He only said “Easy, easy,” the way he spoke to the neighbor's dog, and he said it so often that by the third Sunday she had started saying it to herself.

(5) At the testing center, he handed her the keys and then, after a moment, a second key on a frayed red string.

(6) “Spare,” he said. “In case.”

(7) “In case what?”

(8) He shrugged and looked at the line of cars ahead. “In case.”

(9) She parallel parked on the first try. When she came back to the waiting area with the paper in her hand, he was standing at the window, and she could see the round smudge where his forehead had been pressed against the glass.

(10) “Well?” he said, though he had already seen.

(11) She held up the paper. He nodded once, took the spare key back, and put it in his shirt pocket, patting it twice as though it had done its job.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Okafor's main claim in Passage A?
items.hint: Look at the last sentence of paragraph 1 and the last sentence of paragraph 5. What does Okafor ask the Council to do?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find where Okafor states her position. The last sentence of paragraph 1 says the Council “should pass the proposed ordinance requiring every employer with fifteen or more workers to include a good-faith pay range in each job posting.” Paragraph 5 repeats: “The Council should pass the ordinance.”

Step 2. Match that claim to a choice: requiring employers with fifteen or more workers to list a pay range. Correct.

Step 3. Check the traps. Raising pay is distorted: the ordinance requires posting a range, not paying more. Expanding the pilot is not stated. Learning to negotiate is not stated; Okafor actually argues that secret pay hurts people who are uncomfortable negotiating.
options: The Harlow City Council should require employers with fifteen or more workers to post pay ranges in job ads.
All employers in Harlow, large and small, should be required to raise the starting pay they offer to new workers.
The Workforce Center's pilot program should be expanded to include every employer in Marsh County, not just forty.
Job seekers should learn to negotiate their pay with confidence before they accept any offer from an employer.
why: This is distorted. The ordinance requires employers to post a pay range, not to raise pay, and it covers only employers with fifteen or more workers, not businesses of every size.
This is not stated. Okafor uses the pilot as evidence, but she never asks to expand it. What she asks the Council to do is pass the ordinance.
This is not stated, and it runs against her point. Okafor argues that secret pay hurts people who are not comfortable negotiating; posting the range is her answer to that problem.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2 of Passage B, Whitlock claims that “a posted range locks both sides in before they have even met.” Which type of evidence does he mainly use to support this claim?
items.hint: Reread paragraph 2. Does Whitlock give any numbers, name any experts, or describe a study?
items.explain:
Step 1. List what paragraph 2 contains: a general claim that applicants bring different skills, then the story of the press operator he hired “last spring,” then a guess about what “might have” happened if he had posted a range.

Step 2. The only support is a single personal experience, an anecdote. Correct.

Step 3. Eliminate the rest. Whitlock gives no survey statistics and names no expert. A program in which employers posted ranges is Okafor's evidence (the pilot), not Whitlock's; he mentions it only in paragraph 4, to criticize it.
options: A personal story about one employee he hired
Statistics from a survey of local business owners
Testimony from an expert in labor economics
Results from a program in which employers posted pay
why: Whitlock gives no survey and no numbers. His only mention of other owners is the vague line “many business owners I know agree” in paragraph 3, and that is not statistics.
Whitlock quotes no expert. The only other person in paragraph 2 is the press operator he hired, and that is his own story.
Results from a program are Okafor's evidence (the pilot). Whitlock mentions the pilot only in paragraph 4, and only to criticize it.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from paragraph 2 of Passage A that gives the most specific evidence that posting pay ranges helped employers fill jobs faster.
items.hint: “Filling jobs faster” is about time. Which sentence measures time with numbers?
items.explain:
Step 1. The question asks about filling jobs faster, so the evidence must measure how long hiring took.

Step 2. Only one sentence gives a measured time: “The average time it took them to fill an open position also fell, from 41 days to 33 days.” Correct. That is a drop of 8 days.

Step 3. Check the others. Sentence 1 is the paragraph's claim, not evidence. Sentence 2 describes the pilot but gives no result. Sentence 3 gives a number, but it measures applications from people who turned down offers, not hiring speed. Sentence 5 is related, but “fewer hours” is general and unmeasured, so it is less specific than the 41-to-33-day figure.
spans: Posted pay ranges save time for employers and applicants alike.
Last year, the Workforce Center ran a six-month pilot program in which 40 local employers agreed to list pay ranges in their job ads.
According to the center's final report, those employers received 22 percent fewer applications from people who later turned down an offer because the pay was too low.
The average time it took them to fill an open position also fell, from 41 days to 33 days.
Hiring managers told us they spent fewer hours interviewing candidates who were never going to accept.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the 22 percent sentence, because it has a number in it. That number measures applications from people who later turned down an offer, not how fast jobs were filled.

items.prompt: Which sentence from Passage B is an example of a slippery slope, a claim that one step will inevitably lead to a more extreme result without evidence that it will?
items.hint: Look for a sentence that predicts a chain of events: if this happens, then something bigger will follow.
items.explain:
Step 1. A slippery slope says that step A will lead to a more extreme step B, without showing how or why.

Step 2. “Once the city controls our job ads, it will not be long before it starts telling us what to pay” moves from one step (requiring pay ranges in ads) to a much bigger one (the city setting wages). Whitlock gives no evidence that the second step is planned or likely. Correct.

Step 3. The other sentences are not predictions. “Every applicant brings different skills” is a reasonable general statement. The point about volunteers is a fair criticism of Okafor's evidence. The nineteen-years sentence gives Whitlock's background.
options: “And once the city controls our job ads, it will not be long before it starts telling us what to pay.”
“Every applicant brings different skills and experience to the table.”
“But the 40 employers in that program volunteered, which means they were already comfortable posting pay.”
“I have owned Whitlock Printing on Second Street for nineteen years.”
why: This is a general statement about applicants. It does not predict that one step will lead to a worse one.
This is Whitlock's fair criticism of the pilot. It questions who was in the program; it does not predict a chain of events.
This gives Whitlock's background. It makes no prediction at all.

items.prompt: A learner's thesis states: “Okafor's argument is better supported than Whitlock's.” Select two details from the passages that would best support this thesis in a body paragraph.
items.hint: Choose details that show Okafor using evidence or answering the other side, not details that help Whitlock or only state a value.
items.explain:
Step 1. The thesis is about support, so the best details show Okafor backing her claims with evidence or answering objections.

Step 2. The 41-to-33-day result is measured evidence from a real program. Correct. Okafor's explanation of the fifteen-employee limit and the range requirement directly answers her opponents' concern. Correct.

Step 3. Eliminate the rest. Whitlock's nineteen years and his point about volunteers help his credibility or argument, so they work against this thesis. Okafor's “deserve to know” line and Whitlock's “create the jobs” line are statements of values, not evidence.
options: Okafor reports that during the pilot, the average time to fill an open position fell from 41 days to 33 days.
Okafor answers the worry about small shops by explaining that the ordinance does not apply to businesses with fewer than fifteen employees and requires only a range.
Whitlock has owned his printing business for nineteen years and has hired dozens of people.
Whitlock points out that the employers in the pilot program volunteered to post pay ranges.
Okafor says that job seekers “deserve to know what a job pays.”
Whitlock says that employers “create the jobs this city depends on.”
why: This builds Whitlock's credibility, not Okafor's. It would work against a thesis that Okafor's argument is better supported.
This is Whitlock's best point against Okafor's evidence. It belongs in a concession paragraph that answers it, not as support for Okafor.
This states a value Okafor holds. It tells what she believes, not what she can show, so it is not evidence.
This is Whitlock's statement of a value, and it supports his side, not the thesis.

items.prompt: Which sentence would be the most effective thesis statement for a response to the prompt: “Analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported”?
items.hint: The prompt asks which position is better supported. A strong thesis takes a side on that question and previews the reasons.
items.explain:
Step 1. The prompt asks you to judge which argument is better supported, not which side you agree with.

Step 2. The thesis that cites Okafor's pilot results and her answers to critics names the better-supported argument and previews two reasons based on the quality of the evidence. Correct.

Step 3. “Workers deserve to know what a job pays” gives the writer's own opinion on the issue instead of evaluating the arguments; this is the most common and most costly thesis mistake. “Both writers make some good points” never takes a position. “This essay will discuss” only announces the topic.
options: Okafor's argument is better supported because she uses results from a real pilot and answers her critics, while Whitlock relies on one story and guesses.
Employers should have to post pay ranges in every job ad because workers deserve to know what a job pays before they spend time applying.
Both writers make some good points about pay ranges, and each of the two arguments has real strengths and real weaknesses that readers should carefully weigh.
This essay will discuss two articles about whether job ads in Harlow should include pay ranges and will explain what each of the writers says.
why: This argues the issue (whether pay ranges are good) instead of judging which writer supports a position better. It also names no evidence from either passage.
This never takes a position. The prompt asks you to decide which argument is better supported, and calling it even does not answer the task.
This only announces the topic. A thesis must make a judgment and preview the reasons for it.

items.prompt:
Read the draft response. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): {{0}} the employers in her pilot program posted pay ranges, they received 22 percent fewer applications from people who would reject the pay and filled jobs faster, with the average time to fill a position dropping from 41 days to 33 days.

Paragraph 2, blank (B): These numbers {{1}} her claim that pay ranges make hiring both faster and fairer.
items.hint: For (A), ask how the two parts of the sentence are related: does the first part cause the second or contrast with it? For (B), find the subject and decide whether it is singular or plural.
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: The sentence has two parts: the pilot employers posted pay ranges, and they then received fewer applications from people who would reject the pay and filled jobs faster. Step 2: The first part explains why the second happened, which is exactly Okafor's argument, so a cause word is needed. Step 3: “Because the employers in her pilot program posted pay ranges, they received … and filled jobs faster” makes a complete sentence. Correct. “Although” signals a contrast that is not there. “However,” and “Instead,” would turn the sentence into two independent clauses joined only by a comma (a comma splice), and neither shows cause.

Blank (B). Step 1: The subject is “These numbers,” which is plural. Step 2: The draft is written in the present tense. Step 3: A plural present-tense verb is needed: “These numbers support.” Correct. “Supports” is singular. “Supporting” cannot be the main verb and leaves a fragment. “Has supported” is singular.

options: Because
Although
However,
Instead,
why: “Although” signals a contrast, but there is none here: posting ranges is what caused the fewer refusals and faster hiring.
“However,” signals a contrast that is not there, and with only a comma it joins two complete sentences, which makes a comma splice.
“Instead,” signals a replacement, which makes no sense here, and with only a comma it also creates a comma splice.

options: support
supports
supporting
has supported
why: “Supports” is the singular form. The subject is “These numbers,” which is plural, so the verb must be “support.”
“Supporting” cannot be the main verb of a sentence. “These numbers supporting her claim” is a fragment.
“Has” is singular, but the subject “These numbers” is plural. A plural subject would need “have,” and the draft's present tense calls for “support.”

items.prompt: Which sentence in the draft response should be deleted because it states the writer's personal opinion on the issue instead of evaluating the two arguments?
items.hint: The task is to judge which argument is better supported. Which sentence is about the writer's own feelings instead of the writers' evidence?
items.explain:
Step 1. A GED response evaluates the arguments. It does not argue the issue from the writer's own experience.

Step 2. “Personally, I think every job ad should list the pay, because I hate wasting time on applications” is about the writer's own preference. It adds nothing to the case that Okafor's evidence is stronger. Correct: delete it.

Step 3. The other three sentences all do the job: one introduces the paragraph's point about Okafor's evidence, one cites specific evidence from Passage A, and one explains why Whitlock's anecdote is weak.
options: “Personally, I think every job ad should list the pay, because I hate wasting time on applications.”
“Okafor's evidence comes from a real test, not a guess.”
“Okafor also cites a county review showing that the pay gap between men and women hired into the same jobs was about half as large at employers that posted ranges.”
“He describes hiring a press operator who had more experience than he expected, but one story about one hire cannot show what will happen across a whole city.”
why: This is the topic sentence of paragraph 2. It makes a point about the quality of Okafor's evidence, which is exactly the job of a body paragraph.
This cites specific evidence from Passage A, the county review. Deleting it would weaken the paragraph.
This explains why Whitlock's evidence is weak. It evaluates the argument, so it belongs.

items.prompt: Each sentence below comes from a response about Passages A and B. Drag each sentence to the part of the response where it belongs.
items.hint: Introductions set up the issue. Body paragraphs give and explain specific evidence. Conclusions wrap up the judgment.
items.explain:
Introduction: The sentence about the question the Council must decide frames the issue and names both sides. It gives no evidence, so it belongs at the start.

Body paragraph: “For example, Okafor reports …” gives specific evidence. “Whitlock, on the other hand, supports his claim with a single story” evaluates the other writer's evidence. “This evidence matters because …” explains evidence. Evidence and explanation are the work of body paragraphs.

Conclusion: “In the end, measured results outweigh one owner's predictions …” sums up the judgment. The signal phrase “In the end” and the summary of both sides mark it as a conclusion.
choices: Whether employers should have to list pay in job ads is a question the Harlow City Council must now decide, and the two writers take opposite sides.
For example, Okafor reports that the average time to fill a job dropped from 41 days to 33 days during the pilot.
Whitlock, on the other hand, supports his claim with a single story about hiring one press operator.
This evidence matters because it comes from a real program with 40 employers, not from a guess.
In the end, measured results outweigh one owner's predictions, so Okafor makes the stronger case.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the opening sentence about the Council's decision into a body paragraph. It frames the issue and gives no evidence, so it belongs in the introduction.

items.prompt:
Choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts from the draft response.

Paragraph 3, blank (C): He also predicts that the ordinance will lead the city to control {{0}} no evidence for this prediction.

Paragraph 3, blank (D): To be fair, Whitlock makes one strong point: the employers in the pilot volunteered, so {{1}} results may not apply to every business.

Paragraph 4, blank (E): The {{2}} should look closely at the evidence each writer provides.
items.hint: (C) joins two complete thoughts. (D) needs a word that shows ownership. (E) is the official name of a specific government body.
items.explain:
Blank (C). Step 1: “He also predicts that the ordinance will lead the city to control wages” and “he offers no evidence for this prediction” are both independent clauses. Step 2: Two independent clauses need a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (or a period or semicolon). Step 3: “wages, but he offers” is correct. “wages, he offers” is a comma splice. “wages he offers” is a run-on. “wages. But, he offering” leaves a fragment because “offering” cannot be the main verb.

Blank (D). The results belong to the employers, so the possessive their is correct. “There” refers to a place, “they're” means “they are,” and “it's” means “it is.”

Blank (E). “Harlow City Council” is the official name of a specific body, so every word is capitalized: Harlow City Council. The other choices leave one or more words of the proper name lowercase.

options: wages, but he offers
wages, he offers
wages he offers
wages. But, he offering
why: This is a comma splice: two complete sentences joined by only a comma. Keep the comma and add “but,” or use a period.
This is a run-on: two complete sentences run together with no punctuation and no joining word.
The period ends the first sentence correctly, but “But, he offering no evidence” has no real verb. “Offering” cannot be the main verb, so this is a fragment.

options: their
there
they're
it's
why: “There” points to a place or starts a sentence (“There is…”). The results belong to the employers, so the possessive “their” is needed.
“They're” means “they are.” “They are results may not apply” makes no sense; the sentence needs ownership.
“It's” means “it is,” and it refers to one thing. The results belong to the employers, so use the plural possessive “their.”

options: Harlow City Council
Harlow city council
harlow City Council
Harlow City council
why: “City Council” is part of the official name of one specific body, so both words take capital letters.
Harlow is the name of a city, a proper noun, so it must start with a capital letter.
“Council” is part of the proper name too. Every word in the official name is capitalized.

items.prompt: The writer wants to replace the last sentence of the draft, “That is my opinion about the two articles,” with a stronger concluding sentence. Which choice best does this?
items.hint: A strong concluding sentence restates the judgment and the reasons. It does not add new points or back away from the thesis.
items.explain:
Step 1. A conclusion should restate the thesis in fresh words and remind the reader of the main reasons. It should not introduce new evidence or change positions.

Step 2. The sentence “Okafor backs her claims with tested results and answers her critics, while Whitlock offers one story and guesses…” restates the judgment and sums up the reasons on both sides. Correct.

Step 3. The sentence praising Whitlock's “create the jobs” line adds a new point that contradicts the thesis. The sentence about pay-range laws spreading across the country brings in outside speculation. “Readers should … decide for themselves” abandons the writer's own judgment, which weakens the whole response.
options: Okafor backs her claims with tested results and answers her critics, while Whitlock offers one story and guesses, so her argument is the better supported.
Whitlock also says that employers create the jobs the city depends on, which is one more strong reason the Council should listen closely to his view.
Pay-range laws are becoming more common across the country, and someday soon every job ad in America may be required to list a salary.
In the end, readers should study both of the articles carefully and then decide for themselves which of the two writers is right.
why: This adds a new point, and it contradicts the thesis by praising Whitlock. A conclusion restates your judgment; it does not switch sides.
This brings in outside speculation that neither passage discusses. A conclusion sums up your reasons; it does not add new ideas.
This gives up the writer's own judgment. The task is to decide which argument is better supported, so the conclusion must say which one is.

items.prompt: Which statement best evaluates Whitlock's criticism of the pilot program in paragraph 4 of Passage B?
items.hint: Ask two questions: Is the point about volunteers reasonable? Does Whitlock give any evidence that forced posting would turn out differently?
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify the criticism. Whitlock says the 40 employers volunteered, so they were already comfortable posting pay, and their results may not predict what happens when every business must post.

Step 2. Judge it. That is a fair question about a volunteer group. But Whitlock goes further, saying the pilot “tells us nothing,” and he offers no numbers or examples showing that required posting would lead to different results. So the criticism is fair but overstated and unsupported. Correct.

Step 3. The criticism does not prove the results false; it questions how widely they apply. It addresses the evidence, not Okafor as a person, so it is not a personal attack. Whitlock gives no statistics at all.
options: It raises a fair question about whether the results apply to all employers, but it overstates the point and offers no evidence of different results.
It proves that the pilot results were false, so Okafor's main evidence can no longer be trusted by readers, by employers, or by the members of the Council.
It is a personal attack on Okafor's character and motives rather than a response to the evidence that she presents in her article.
It relies on statistics from Whitlock's own printing business that contradict the main findings of the Workforce Center's pilot program.
why: This overstates the criticism. Whitlock questions whether volunteers' results apply to everyone; he gives no evidence that the results were false.
Whitlock never mentions Okafor or her character. He criticizes who was in the pilot, which is a response to evidence, not a personal attack.
Whitlock gives no statistics at all, from his business or anywhere else. That missing evidence is exactly the weakness of his criticism.

items.prompt:
Read this body paragraph from a learner's response to Passages A and B.

Pay ranges in job ads are a fair and sensible idea. When workers know the pay in advance, they can plan their lives and avoid wasting their time. Employers also benefit, since they can attract serious applicants. For these reasons, the City Council should pass the ordinance.

Complete the scorer's note.

If the whole response were written like this paragraph, its weakest trait would be {{0}}, because the paragraph {{1}}. The revision that would most improve that score is to {{2}}.
items.hint: Ask of each trait: Is the paragraph organized? Is it written correctly? Does it judge the two writers' evidence?
items.explain:
Step 1. Check each trait. The sentences are correct and clear (Trait 3 is fine). The paragraph has a topic sentence, logical order, and a transition (Trait 2 is fine).

Step 2. Trait 1 asks whether the response makes an argument about which position is better supported and backs it with specific evidence from the passages. This paragraph argues the issue itself (“Pay ranges … are a fair and sensible idea”) and never mentions Okafor, Whitlock, the pilot, or any detail from either passage. Trait 1 is the weakest.

Step 3. The fix is to bring in specific evidence from both passages and explain why Okafor's is stronger. A personal story is the most tempting wrong fix, but it moves the response further from the task.

options: Trait 1 (arguments and use of evidence)
Trait 2 (development and organization)
Trait 3 (clarity and standard English)
why: Trait 2 is not the main problem. The paragraph has a clear topic sentence, sentences in a logical order, and a transition (“For these reasons”).
Trait 3 is not the main problem. The sentences are clear, varied, and free of grammar and punctuation errors.

options: argues that pay ranges are good instead of judging whose support is stronger, and cites nothing from either passage
is full of grammar and punctuation errors that make its sentences hard to follow and understand
jumps from one idea to another without a topic sentence or any transitions between the sentences
spends too much time quoting the passages instead of explaining the quotations in its own words
why: Check the sentences again: they are correct and easy to read. The problem is what the paragraph argues, not how it is written.
The paragraph opens with a topic sentence and uses the transition “For these reasons.” Its organization is fine.
The paragraph does not quote the passages at all. The problem is the opposite: it has no evidence from them.

options: name specific evidence from both passages and explain why Okafor's is stronger
add transition words such as “furthermore” and “moreover” to every sentence
check the spelling of each writer's name and capitalize “City Council”
add a personal story about a time when a job ad left out the pay
why: The paragraph already flows. More transition words will not fix the real problem: it never judges the two writers' evidence.
Spelling and capitals are Trait 3, which is already strong here. The weak trait needs evidence and evaluation.
A personal story pulls the response even further away from the task. The response must judge the passages' support, not the writer's own experience.

items.prompt: In paragraph 8, why does Marisol mop “the same clean square twice”?
items.hint: The end of the sentence tells you why. What is she listening to, and how does she seem to feel about it?
items.explain:
Step 1. Reread the sentence: “she found she was mopping the same clean square twice just to keep listening.” The words “just to keep listening” give the reason.

Step 2. What is she listening to? “The scratch of his pencil, steady as rain on the awning.” Teo is finally studying, after telling her he could move up to the advanced class. She slows down and stays near him. The gentle comparison to rain shows the sound comforts her. Correct: she wants to keep hearing her son study, and it pleases her.

Step 3. The tiredness choice is tempting because it is late at night, but the passage states a different reason. Her father taught her how to mop, not to mop twice. And by this point there is no sign she is upset with Teo.
options: She wants to stay close and keep hearing her son study, which quietly pleases her.
She is so tired at the end of the night that she has lost track of her cleaning.
She is following her father's strict rule that every square of floor be mopped twice.
She is still upset that Teo ignored her earlier and wants him to notice her work.
why: This is not supported. The passage gives the reason directly: she mops the square twice “just to keep listening.” Nothing suggests she is confused.
This is distorted. Her father taught her to mop in “long, even strokes,” but the passage never mentions a rule about mopping twice.
This is not supported. By paragraph 8 Teo has opened the book as she asked, and she works around his stool so she will not disturb him.

items.skill: Literary analysis: purpose of a detail
items.prompt: What does the description of Marisol's father in paragraph 4 mainly suggest?
items.hint: Look at what the father paid attention to and what he saved. What does that suggest about the business, and why might Marisol keep the shoebox closed?
items.explain:
Step 1. List the details: her father read prices out loud “as if the numbers were news from a distant country”; “Eggs, up again. Flour, up again”; he “kept every receipt in a shoebox”; Marisol still has the shoebox but has “stopped opening it.”

Step 2. Rising costs and saving every receipt show that running the diner was a careful, worried business. Marisol keeping the shoebox, but not opening it, suggests she still holds those worries without wanting to look at them. Correct.

Step 3. The “wealthy businessman” choice misreads the newspaper detail; he read grocery prices, not investments. The selling and accounting choices add ideas the story never states.
options: Running the diner has long been a hard, careful living, and Marisol still carries her father's worries.
Marisol's father was a wealthy businessman who enjoyed tracking the value of his investments in the daily newspaper.
Marisol plans to sell the diner soon because the rising price of eggs and flour has made it impossible to stay open.
Marisol's father wanted her to study accounting so that she would not have to work late nights at the diner.
why: This is distorted. He read the prices of eggs and flour, the costs of running a diner, and kept every receipt; nothing suggests wealth or investments.
This is not stated. Rising prices are mentioned, but nothing in the passage says Marisol plans to sell or close the diner.
This is not stated. The passage never mentions accounting or any plans her father had for her career.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Fortier's main claim in Passage A?
items.hint: Look at the last sentence of paragraph 1 and the last sentence of paragraph 5. What does Fortier ask the Council to do?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find where Fortier states her position. The last sentence of paragraph 1 says, “The City Council should make all city buses fare-free starting next July.” Paragraph 5 repeats it: “The Council should vote yes.”

Step 2. Match that claim to a choice: making all city buses fare-free. Correct.

Step 3. Check the traps. Raising property taxes is distorted; Fortier says no new tax is needed, and it is Parrish who predicts higher taxes. Extending the trial is not stated. Telling commuters to ride the bus is a detail turned into a claim she never makes.
options: The Eastvale City Council should make all city buses fare-free starting next July.
Eastvale should raise property taxes to buy newer buses and build better shelters.
The fare-free trial on Route 4 should be extended for six more months of study.
Commuters in Eastvale should leave their cars at home and ride the bus to work.
why: This is distorted. Fortier says the opposite about taxes: “No new tax is required.” Shelters and newer buses are Parrish's concerns, not her claim.
This is not stated. Fortier uses the trial as evidence for making every bus free; she never asks to extend the trial.
This is too narrow and not her claim. She reports that many new riders had been driving, but she asks the Council to act, not commuters.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2 of Passage B, Parrish claims that free buses will make regular riders “stop feeling safe.” Which type of evidence does he mainly use to support this claim?
items.hint: Reread paragraph 2 of Passage B. Does Parrish give any numbers, quote anyone, or describe a study?
items.explain:
Step 1. List what paragraph 2 of Passage B contains: a general claim (“Free service changes who rides”), one observation (a man riding Route 4 three times “to stay out of the heat”), and a prediction (“regular riders will stop feeling safe”).

Step 2. The only support is a single thing he saw, an anecdote. Correct. Notice that nothing in his story shows anyone feeling unsafe; the prediction goes beyond even his one example.

Step 3. Parrish gives no statistics, quotes no officer, and cites no survey. The survey belongs to Fortier's passage.
options: One thing he saw a single rider do on one afternoon
Crime statistics reported by the Transit Department
Testimony from a police officer who patrols Route 4
A survey of riders that was taken during the trial
why: Parrish gives no statistics at all. The only Transit Department numbers in either passage come from Fortier.
Parrish quotes no police officer or other expert. The only person in paragraph 2 is the man he watched ride the bus.
A rider survey is Fortier's evidence (paragraph 2 of Passage A). Parrish never mentions a survey.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from paragraph 2 of Passage A that gives the most specific evidence that free fares drew people out of their cars.
items.hint: Being drawn “out of their cars” means the riders used to drive. Which sentence tells how new riders traveled before?
items.explain:
Step 1. The question is about people leaving their cars, so the evidence must say something about how new riders used to travel.

Step 2. Only one sentence does: “A rider survey taken during the trial found that 38 percent of new riders had previously driven alone to work or school.” Correct.

Step 3. The first sentence is the paragraph's claim, not evidence. The second describes the trial but gives no result. The 31 percent sentence is strong evidence that ridership grew, but it does not show that the new riders had been driving.
spans: Free fares bring more riders onto the bus.
From March through August of last year, the city ran a fare-free trial on Route 4, its busiest line.

According to the Eastvale Transit Department's report on the trial, weekday ridership on Route 4 rose 31 percent compared with the same months the year before, while ridership on the city's other routes, which still charged fares, rose 2 percent.
A rider survey taken during the trial found that 38 percent of new riders had previously driven alone to work or school.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the 31 percent sentence. It shows that more people rode the bus, but it says nothing about where those riders came from. Only the survey sentence shows that many new riders used to drive.

items.prompt: Which sentence from Passage B is an example of a slippery slope, a claim that one step will inevitably lead to a more extreme result without evidence that it will?
items.hint: Look for a sentence that predicts a chain of events: if this happens, then something bigger and worse will follow.
items.explain:
Step 1. A slippery slope says that step A will lead to a more extreme step B (and maybe C), without showing how or why.

Step 2. The sentence about riders expecting “free buses forever” moves from one step (free fares) to a much bigger one (higher property taxes on every homeowner), and Parrish ignores Fortier's plan to use parking-meter money. He gives no evidence that the chain will happen. Correct.

Step 3. The shelters sentence states a need. The March-through-August sentence is the fairest point in his letter, a criticism of the evidence. The twenty-two-years sentence gives his background.
options: “Once riders get used to paying nothing, they will expect free buses forever, and the only way to keep paying for them will be to raise property taxes on every homeowner in Eastvale.”
“Eastvale's buses need better shelters, newer vehicles, and more frequent service.”

“But the trial ran only from March through August, when school was out for part of the time, the weather was mild, and the newness of a free bus drew curious riders who will not keep riding once the excitement wears off.”
“I have run Parrish Hardware on Mill Street for twenty-two years, and the Route 4 bus stops right outside my door.”
why: This states a need. It may be true, and it predicts nothing about one step leading to another.
This is Parrish's criticism of the trial's timing. It questions the evidence; it does not claim that free fares will set off a chain of worse events.
This gives Parrish's background. It makes no prediction at all.

items.prompt: A learner's thesis states: “Fortier's argument is better supported than Parrish's.” Select two details from the passages that would best support this thesis in a body paragraph.
items.hint: Choose details that show Fortier using measured evidence or answering an objection, not details that help Parrish or only restate a claim.
items.explain:
Step 1. The thesis is about support, so the best details show Fortier backing her claims with evidence or answering the other side.

Step 2. The on-time figures (71 to 84 percent) are measured results from the trial. Correct. The $820,000 figure and the parking-meter plan directly answer the critics' main question: how would the city pay? Correct.

Step 3. Parrish's twenty-two years and his point about the trial's timing help his side. Fortier's “small charge” line is a claim, not proof. Parrish's list of needs supports his side.
options: Fortier reports that during the trial, the share of Route 4 trips arriving on time rose from 71 percent to 84 percent.
Fortier answers the cost concern by showing that the real cost would be about $820,000 a year, which parking-meter revenue could cover.
Parrish has run his hardware store on Mill Street for twenty-two years, with the Route 4 stop outside his door.
Parrish points out that the trial ran for only six warm months on a single route.
Fortier says a bus fare is “a small charge that keeps people off the bus.”
Parrish says Eastvale's buses need “better shelters, newer vehicles, and more frequent service.”
why: This builds Parrish's credibility as someone who sees the bus every day. It does not support a thesis that Fortier's argument is better supported.
This is Parrish's best point against Fortier's evidence. It belongs in a concession paragraph that answers it, not as support for Fortier.
This restates Fortier's claim in strong words. It is what she believes, not the evidence that proves it.
This is Parrish's statement of what the buses need. It supports his side, and it is not evidence about either writer's support.

items.prompt: Which sentence would be the most effective thesis statement for a response to the prompt: “Analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported”?
items.hint: The prompt asks which position is better supported. A strong thesis takes a side on that question and previews the reasons.
items.explain:
Step 1. The prompt asks which position is better supported, so the thesis must name a writer and preview reasons about the quality of support.

Step 2. The thesis naming Fortier's trial results and her cost plan, and Parrish's single story and guesses, does both. Correct.

Step 3. “Eastvale should keep charging bus fares” is tempting because it sounds confident and uses details from Passage B, but it argues the issue instead of judging the arguments. The “both care” thesis takes no position. The “In this response, I will discuss” thesis only announces the topic.
options: Fortier's argument is better supported because she uses results from a real trial and shows how to pay for free fares, while Parrish relies on one story and guesses.
Eastvale should keep charging bus fares, because nothing is truly free and the city's buses badly need new shelters, newer vehicles, and much more frequent service.
Fortier and Parrish both care about Eastvale's buses, and each of them makes several strong points and several weak points that are worth thinking about.
In this response, I will discuss two articles about whether the buses in Eastvale should be free and will describe what each of the writers believes.
why: This argues the issue (whether fares should stay) from the writer's own point of view. The task is to judge which writer's argument is better supported.
This never takes a position. Saying both writers have strong and weak points does not answer which one is better supported.
This only announces the topic and promises a summary. A thesis must make a judgment and preview the reasons.

items.prompt:
Read the draft response. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): {{0}} weekday ridership on Route 4 rose 31 percent during the fare-free months, ridership on the routes that still charged fares rose only 2 percent.

Paragraph 2, blank (B): These results {{1}} her claim that free fares bring in riders and speed up service.
items.hint: For (A), are the two numbers alike, or are they being contrasted? For (B), find the subject and decide whether it is singular or plural.
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: The sentence puts two numbers side by side: Route 4 rose 31 percent; the routes with fares rose only 2 percent. The word “only” shows they are being contrasted. Step 2: A contrast word that can begin a dependent clause is needed. Step 3: “While weekday ridership on Route 4 rose 31 percent …, ridership on the routes that still charged fares rose only 2 percent” is a complete, correct sentence. Correct. “Because” shows cause, which is wrong here. “Therefore,” and “Similarly,” show the wrong relationships and leave a comma splice.

Blank (B). The subject is “These results,” which is plural, and the draft is in the present tense, so the verb must be “These results strengthen.” “Strengthens” and “has strengthened” are singular, and “strengthening” leaves a fragment.

options: While
Because
Therefore,
Similarly,
why: “Because” says the first part caused the second. Route 4's ridership rising did not cause the other routes to rise only 2 percent; the sentence sets two numbers side by side to contrast them.
“Therefore,” signals a result, which does not fit, and with only a comma it joins two complete sentences, a comma splice.
“Similarly,” signals that two things are alike, but 31 percent and 2 percent are being contrasted. With only a comma it also makes a comma splice.

options: strengthen
strengthens
strengthening
has strengthened
why: “Strengthens” is singular. The subject is “These results,” which is plural, so the verb must be “strengthen.”
“Strengthening” cannot be the main verb. “These results strengthening her claim” is a fragment.
“Has” is singular, but “These results” is plural. A plural subject would need “have,” and the draft's present tense calls for “strengthen.”

items.prompt: Which sentence in the draft response should be deleted because it uses the writer's personal experience instead of evaluating the two arguments?
items.hint: The task is to judge which argument is better supported. Which sentence is about someone in the writer's own life instead of the passages?
items.explain:
Step 1. A GED response evaluates the arguments in the passages. Stories from the writer's own life do not show which passage is better supported.

Step 2. The sentence about the writer's cousin brings in outside, personal evidence and argues the issue (free fares save money). It does nothing to show that Fortier's support is stronger. Correct: delete it.

Step 3. The other three sentences each do a job: one states the paragraph's point about Fortier's evidence, one cites specific evidence from Passage A, and one explains why Parrish's anecdote is weak.
options: “My cousin rides the bus every day, and she says free fares would save her a lot of money.”
“Fortier's evidence comes from a real trial, not a guess.”
“Fortier also reports that the average time a bus spent at each stop fell from 18 seconds to 11 seconds.”
“He describes one man who rode the bus to stay out of the heat, but one rider on one afternoon cannot show how thousands of riders will behave.”
why: This is the topic sentence of paragraph 2. It makes a point about the quality of Fortier's evidence, which is the job of a body paragraph.
This cites specific, accurate evidence from Passage A. Deleting it would weaken the paragraph.
This explains why Parrish's evidence is weak. It evaluates the argument, so it belongs.

items.prompt: Each sentence below comes from a response about the Eastvale bus-fare passages. Drag each sentence to the part of the response where it belongs.
items.hint: Introductions set up the issue. Body paragraphs give and explain specific evidence. Conclusions wrap up the judgment.
items.explain:
Introduction: The sentence about the question the Council must decide frames the issue and names both sides. It gives no evidence, so it belongs at the start.

Body paragraph: “For example, Fortier reports …” gives specific evidence. “Parrish, by contrast, supports his claim with the story of one man …” evaluates the other writer's evidence. “This comparison matters because …” explains evidence. Giving and explaining evidence is the work of body paragraphs.

Conclusion: “In the end, measured results outweigh one shop owner's predictions …” sums up the judgment. The signal phrase “In the end” and the summary of both sides mark it as the conclusion.
choices: Whether Eastvale should make its buses free is a question the City Council must soon decide, and the two writers take opposite sides.
For example, Fortier reports that buses spent an average of 11 seconds at each stop during the trial, down from 18.
Parrish, by contrast, supports his claim with the story of one man who rode Route 4 to stay out of the heat.
This comparison matters because the routes that still charged fares grew by only 2 percent in the same months.
In the end, measured results outweigh one shop owner's predictions, so Fortier makes the stronger case.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the sentence that begins “In the end” into a body paragraph because it mentions evidence. It sums up the judgment for the whole response and adds nothing new, so it is the conclusion.

items.prompt:
Choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts from the draft response.

Paragraph 3, blank (C): He also predicts that free buses will force the city to raise property {{0}} offers no evidence for this prediction.

Paragraph 3, blank (D): To be fair, Parrish makes one reasonable point: the trial lasted only six warm months on one route, so {{1}} results might not hold for a full year.

Paragraph 4, blank (E): The {{2}} should weigh the evidence carefully before it votes.
items.hint: (C) joins two complete thoughts. (D) needs a word that shows ownership by one thing. (E) is the official name of a specific government body.
items.explain:
Blank (C). “He also predicts that free buses will force the city to raise property taxes” and “he offers no evidence for this prediction” are both independent clauses. Two independent clauses need a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (or a period or semicolon): “taxes, but he offers.” Correct. “taxes, he” is a comma splice; “taxes he” is a run-on; “Although he offers…” left on its own is a fragment.

Blank (D). The results belong to “the trial,” one thing, so the singular possessive its is correct. “It's” means “it is”; “their” is plural and does not agree with “trial”; “there” is not a possessive.

Blank (E). “Eastvale City Council” is the official name of a specific body, so every word is capitalized: Eastvale City Council.

options: taxes, but he
taxes, he
taxes he
taxes. Although he
why: This is a comma splice: two complete sentences joined by only a comma. Add “but” after the comma, or use a period.
This is a run-on: two complete sentences with no punctuation and no joining word between them.
The period ends the first sentence, but “Although he offers no evidence for this prediction.” is a dependent clause standing alone, which is a fragment.

options: its
it's
their
there
why: “It's” means “it is.” “It is results might not hold” makes no sense; the sentence needs the possessive “its.”
“Their” is plural, but it refers to “the trial,” which is singular. A singular noun takes the singular possessive “its.”
“There” points to a place or starts a sentence (“There is…”). It cannot show that the results belong to the trial.

options: Eastvale City Council
Eastvale city council
eastvale City Council
Eastvale City council
why: “City Council” is part of the official name of one specific body, so both words take capital letters.
Eastvale is the name of a city, a proper noun, so it must be capitalized.
“Council” is part of the proper name too. Every word in the official name is capitalized.

items.prompt: The writer wants to replace the last sentence of the draft, “That is just what I think about it,” with a stronger concluding sentence. Which choice best does this?
items.hint: A strong concluding sentence restates the judgment and the reasons. It does not add new points or back away from the thesis.
items.explain:
Step 1. A strong concluding sentence restates the judgment in fresh words and recalls the main reasons. It adds no new evidence and does not change sides.

Step 2. The sentence “Fortier supports her plan with trial results and a clear way to pay for it, while Parrish offers one story and guesses…” restates the thesis and sums up the reasons on both sides. Correct.

Step 3. The shelters sentence switches to Parrish's side. The sentence about cities around the world adds outside information. “Each reader will have to … decide” abandons the judgment the whole response was built to prove.
options: Fortier supports her plan with trial results and a clear way to pay for it, while Parrish offers one story and guesses, so her argument is better supported.
Parrish is also right that the buses need better shelters and newer vehicles, which is one more strong reason the Council should listen closely to his view.
Many cities around the world have already tried free buses, and in a few years most American cities may stop charging fares as well.
In the end, each reader will have to look at both articles carefully and then decide which one of the two writers is right.
why: This adds a new point and contradicts the thesis by siding with Parrish. A conclusion restates your judgment; it does not switch sides.
This brings in outside claims about other cities that neither passage makes. A conclusion sums up your reasons; it does not add new ones.
This gives up the writer's judgment. The task is to decide which argument is better supported, so the conclusion must say which one is.

items.prompt: Which statement best evaluates Parrish's criticism of the fare-free trial in paragraph 4 of Passage B?
items.hint: Ask two questions: Is the point about the trial's timing reasonable? Does Parrish give any evidence that riders would leave?
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify the criticism. Parrish says the trial ran only from March through August, with mild weather, part of the time without school, and curious first-time riders, so it “cannot tell us” what a full year on every route will look like.

Step 2. Judge it. Questioning a short, seasonal trial on one route is fair. But Parrish gives no numbers showing that riders left after the excitement wore off, and Fortier's comparison already shows that routes with fares grew only 2 percent in the same months. So the point is fair but unsupported. Correct.

Step 3. The criticism does not prove anything false, it does not attack Fortier personally, and Parrish offers no counts of his own.
options: It raises a fair point about the trial's length and timing, but it offers no evidence that ridership would fall once the trial ended.
It proves that the trial's results were false, so none of Fortier's ridership, timing, or cost numbers can be trusted by the Council.
It is a personal attack on Fortier's motives rather than a response to the trial evidence that she presents in her article.
It relies on ridership counts from Parrish's own customers that contradict the main findings of the Transit Department's report.
why: This overstates the criticism. Parrish questions whether six warm months can predict a full year; he offers nothing showing the numbers were false.
Parrish never mentions Fortier or her motives. He criticizes the trial's timing, which is a response to evidence, not a personal attack.
Parrish gives no ridership counts of any kind. His criticism rests on reasons, not on numbers.

items.prompt:
Read this body paragraph from a learner's response to the Eastvale passages.

Fortier's evidence is stronger then Parrish's. She report that ridership on Route 4 rose 31 percent, the other routes only rose 2 percent this shows the free fares made the difference. parrish only tells about one man who rode the bus to stay out of the heat, one man cant show how every rider acts.

Complete the scorer's note.

If the whole response were written like this paragraph, its weakest trait would be {{0}}, because the paragraph {{1}}. The revision that would most improve that score is to {{2}}.
items.hint: This paragraph has real evidence. Read it once only for errors: how many can you find?
items.explain:
Step 1. Check Trait 1: the paragraph judges which writer's evidence is stronger, cites specific evidence from both passages (31 percent and 2 percent; the man riding to stay out of the heat), and explains it. That is solid.

Step 2. Check Trait 2: a clear opening point and a logical order. That is fine.

Step 3. Check Trait 3: “then” should be than; “She report” should be She reports; “rose 31 percent, the other routes” is a comma splice; “2 percent this shows” is a run-on; “parrish” needs a capital; “heat, one man” is another comma splice; “cant” needs an apostrophe. Errors appear in nearly every sentence, so Trait 3 is the weakest, and the fix is a careful edit in the last minutes. Note the contrast with a paragraph that is clean but has no evidence: there, Trait 1 is the problem.

options: Trait 1 (arguments and use of evidence)
Trait 2 (development and organization)
Trait 3 (clarity and standard English)
why: Trait 1 is a strength here. The paragraph judges the support, cites specific numbers from Passage A and the anecdote from Passage B, and explains both.
Trait 2 is reasonable here. The paragraph opens with a clear point and moves logically from Fortier's evidence to Parrish's.

options: has errors in word choice, verb endings, sentence boundaries, and capitals in nearly every sentence
argues that the buses should be free instead of judging which writer's support is stronger
uses no specific evidence from either passage to back up its point about the two writers
has no topic sentence that tells the reader what the paragraph is going to be about
why: Reread it: the paragraph compares the writers' evidence (“Fortier's evidence is stronger”). It does not argue the issue.
It uses specific evidence: 31 percent, 2 percent, and the man who rode to stay out of the heat.
The first sentence is a clear topic sentence, even with its error: “Fortier's evidence is stronger then Parrish's.”

options: edit for confused words, verb endings, run-ons, and capitals in the last minutes
add more numbers from Fortier's article, such as the stop times and on-time rates
move the sentence about Parrish to the start so the paragraph opens with him
replace the anecdote with a story about the writer's own experience on a bus
why: More evidence would help Trait 1, which is already the paragraph's strength. The weak trait is the writing itself.
Reordering the sentences would not fix a single error, and the current order already makes sense.
A personal story would hurt Trait 1 and would still be full of the same errors. Editing is the fix.

items.prompt: In paragraph 9, what does “the round smudge where his forehead had been pressed against the glass” suggest about Grandpa Lewis?
items.hint: What would you have to do to leave a forehead smudge on a window? Connect it to “He never said he was nervous.”
items.explain:
Step 1. Ask what makes a smudge from a forehead: standing with your face pressed to the glass for a long time, trying to see.

Step 2. Connect it to other details. Paragraph 4 says, “He never said he was nervous,” but his hand hovered over the brake “the whole time.” Paragraph 10 says he “had already seen” the result. Together, these show he was watching her test closely and anxiously. Correct.

Step 3. The boredom and sleep choice and the line-of-cars choice both conflict with “he had already seen.” The dirty-windows choice mistakes a clue about his feelings for a literal comment on cleaning.
options: He had been watching Kiara's test anxiously, though he never said he was nervous.
He had grown so bored waiting that he leaned against the window and fell asleep.
He had been looking out at the line of cars and paying no attention to Kiara's test.
He had noticed that the testing center's windows were dirty and wanted to clean them.
why: This is not supported. Nothing suggests sleep; he is standing at the window when she returns and “had already seen” the result.
This is contradicted. He “had already seen” how the test went, so he was watching her, not ignoring her.
This reads the smudge too literally. The smudge was made by his own forehead, which shows how close he stood to watch, not a concern about cleaning.

items.skill: Literary analysis: purpose of a detail
items.prompt: What purpose does the spare key mainly serve in the story?
items.hint: Grandpa Lewis does not say what he feels. How does he show it instead, and how does he treat the key at the end?
items.explain:
Step 1. Gather the details. Grandpa Lewis gives her the key “after a moment,” says only “In case,” and will not say in case of what. Afterward he takes it back and pats it twice “as though it had done its job.”

Step 2. Connect it to his character. Paragraph 4 says “He never said he was nervous”; he shows feelings through actions, like cleaning the car. The key works the same way: a small, practical gesture that carries his care and worry. Correct.

Step 3. The “expects Kiara to fail” choice is tempting because “In case” sounds doubtful, but his pride at the end does not fit. Nothing suggests the car is unreliable, and the story never links the key to her parking.
options: It is a quiet way for Grandpa Lewis to show his care and worry without putting them into words.
It shows that Grandpa Lewis expects Kiara to fail the test and need a second key to try again.
It reveals that the old blue sedan is unreliable and often needs a second key before it will start.
It explains why Kiara was able to stay calm enough to parallel park perfectly on her very first try.
why: This is not supported. He takes the key back and pats it “as though it had done its job,” which suggests it was a comfort, not a plan for failure.
This is not stated. Nothing in the story says the car has trouble starting.
This is distorted. The story never connects the key to her parking. If anything, her calm comes from his “Easy, easy” lessons.

stimuli.title: Two Letters to the Editor: Speed Cameras Near Ridgeview Schools
stimuli.html:
Letter 1: Keep the Cameras on Lincoln Avenue

By Angela Brooks, member of the Ridgeview School Safety Committee

(1) Ridgeview should make its school-zone speed cameras permanent. For eighteen months, the city tested two cameras on Lincoln Avenue, outside Lincoln Elementary. Before the trial, a city traffic study found that 41 percent of drivers in the school zone were going more than 10 miles per hour over the limit during morning arrival and afternoon dismissal. By the end of the trial, that share had fallen to 9 percent.

(2) Fewer speeders means fewer crashes. Police records show 14 crashes in the Lincoln Avenue school zone in the eighteen months before the cameras and 6 in the eighteen months with them.

(3) Some residents worry about privacy. Under the trial rules, the cameras photograph only the license plates of speeding vehicles, and every image is deleted within 30 days unless it is needed for a ticket. Ticket money pays for two crossing guards; none of it goes into the city's general budget.

Letter 2: Cameras Are About Cash, Not Kids

By Ray Dunham, Ridgeview resident

(1) Speed cameras are a money grab, plain and simple. My neighbor got a $75 ticket for going 31 in a 20 zone at 7:50 in the morning, and he says there wasn't a child in sight. Everyone on my street knows the cameras are about cash, not kids.

(2) Make these cameras permanent, and soon there will be one on every corner of Ridgeview, watching where we go day and night.

(3) Cameras also do nothing in the moment. A ticket arrives in the mail weeks later. By then, the driver who sped past the crosswalk is long gone. A crossing guard or a police officer can stop a dangerous driver on the spot.
stimuli.source: Original letters written for KCE GED Prep

stimuli.title: Draft Body Paragraph: Speed Cameras
stimuli.html:
A learner wrote this body paragraph about the two speed-camera letters. It has not been edited. Blanks (A) through (C) mark places to be edited.

(1) Brooks's letter is better supported than Dunham's. (2) Brooks reports that the share of drivers speeding in the school zone fell from 41 percent to 9 percent during the trial. (3) The number of crashes in the zone also (A) from 14 to 6. (4) (B) Dunham supports his claim with one ticket his neighbor received. (5) One ticket on one morning cannot prove that the cameras are a money grab, and Dunham never explains how he knows what (C) neighbors think.

stimuli.title: The Interview
stimuli.source: Original short story written for KCE GED Prep
stimuli.html:
Denise arrived twenty minutes early and sat in the car with the engine off, reading her own résumé as if it belonged to a stranger. Warehouse lead, six years. Forklift certified. Trained eleven new hires. She had written those lines at the kitchen table at midnight, crossing out “helped” and writing “trained,” crossing out “worked” and writing “led.” Each change had felt like a small lie.

Now, in the parking lot, she read the lines again, slowly, and found she could remember each of the eleven: their names, their first clumsy weeks, the morning Luis finally backed the forklift into the bay without a single correction. She folded the résumé once, put it in her bag, and checked her face in the mirror. Then she got out of the car.

stimuli.title: Two Letters to the Editor: Uniforms in Clearwater Middle Schools
stimuli.html:
Letter 1: Uniforms Are Working at Jefferson

By Monica Hale, PTA president at Jefferson Middle School

(1) The Clearwater school board should adopt uniforms at all three of its middle schools. Jefferson Middle School switched to uniforms two years ago. In the year before the change, the school recorded 312 discipline referrals. In its second year with uniforms, it recorded 205.

(2) Uniforms also ease the pressure on family budgets. In a PTA survey answered by 280 Jefferson families, 71 percent said they spent less on school clothes after the change.

(3) Some parents worry about the cost of buying uniforms. Jefferson's uniform closet gives free uniforms to any family that asks, and last year it gave out 400 donated sets.

Letter 2: Let Kids Be Themselves

By Curtis Lowe, Clearwater parent

(1) Uniforms crush kids' creativity. My daughter loves to design her own outfits, and at a uniform school she would have no way to show who she is. Every parent I have talked to agrees that uniforms are a bad idea.

(2) Today it is shirts and pants. Next the board will be telling our kids how to wear their hair and what to pack in their lunch boxes.

(3) Supporters brag about Jefferson's drop in referrals, but Jefferson also hired a full-time counselor the same year it adopted uniforms. The school's own staff list shows the counselor started that August. Nobody can say which change made the difference.
stimuli.source: Original letters written for KCE GED Prep

stimuli.title: Draft Body Paragraph: School Uniforms
stimuli.html:
A learner wrote this body paragraph about the two uniform letters. It has not been edited. Blanks (A) through (C) mark places to be edited.

(1) Hale's letter is better supported than Lowe's. (2) Hale reports that discipline referrals at Jefferson dropped from 312 in the year before uniforms to 205 in the second year with them. (3) A PTA survey of 280 families (A) that 71 percent spent less on school clothes. (4) (B) Lowe supports his claim with the example of his own daughter. (5) One child's love of designing outfits cannot show how uniforms affect a whole district, and Lowe never says how many parents (C) talked to.

stimuli.title: First Paycheck
stimuli.source: Original short story written for KCE GED Prep
stimuli.html:
The envelope sat on the kitchen table all evening, propped against the sugar bowl where Marcus had left it. His mother walked past it twice while she made dinner and did not touch it. His little sister asked what it was, and he said, “Nothing,” and then, a minute later, “My check from the grocery.” During dinner nobody mentioned it.

Afterward, while his mother washed the pots, Marcus opened the envelope, counted the amount twice, and slid two twenties under the edge of the sugar bowl. In the morning the twenties were gone. In their place was a note in his mother's slanted handwriting: “For your first car. I'm keeping it for you.” Under the note was the small key to the metal cash box she kept on the top shelf of the hall closet.

items.prompt: A learner is writing an Extended Response about the two speed-camera letters. Which thesis statement would best begin a high-scoring response?
items.explain: The prompt asks which position is better supported. The Brooks thesis names the better-supported letter and previews reasons about the quality of evidence: an eighteen-month trial with measured results, an answer to the privacy concern, and Dunham's reliance on one ticket. The thesis calling for Ridgeview to get rid of its cameras is the most tempting wrong answer because it sounds strong, but it argues the issue rather than evaluating the two letters. The other two choices take no position.
options: Brooks's letter is better supported because she gives measured results from a long trial and answers the privacy worry, while Dunham relies on one ticket.
Ridgeview should get rid of its school-zone speed cameras, because a ticket that arrives in the mail weeks later can never stop a dangerous driver at a crosswalk.
Brooks and Dunham both care about keeping Ridgeview's children safe, and each of their letters has some strong points and some weak points that are worth weighing.
This response will look at two letters about the speed cameras near Ridgeview's schools and will explain in detail what each of the two writers happens to believe.
why: This argues the issue (get rid of the cameras) instead of judging which letter is better supported. It borrows Dunham's point as if it were the writer's own opinion.
This never takes a position. The task is to decide which argument is better supported, so a thesis that calls it even does not answer the prompt.
This only announces the topic and promises a summary. A thesis must state a judgment and preview the reasons.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from Brooks's letter that gives the most specific evidence that the cameras reduced crashes in the school zone.
items.explain: The question asks about crashes, so the evidence must count crashes. “Police records show 14 crashes … before the cameras and 6 … with them” does exactly that, for equal eighteen-month periods, from an official source. “Fewer speeders means fewer crashes” is a claim, not evidence. The 41 percent and 9 percent sentences measure speeding, which is related but is not the same as crashes.
spans: Ridgeview should make its school-zone speed cameras permanent.
For eighteen months, the city tested two cameras on Lincoln Avenue, outside Lincoln Elementary.
Before the trial, a city traffic study found that 41 percent of drivers in the school zone were going more than 10 miles per hour over the limit during morning arrival and afternoon dismissal.
By the end of the trial, that share had fallen to 9 percent.
Fewer speeders means fewer crashes.
Police records show 14 crashes in the Lincoln Avenue school zone in the eighteen months before the cameras and 6 in the eighteen months with them.
Some residents worry about privacy.
items.why: The most common wrong click is “By the end of the trial, that share had fallen to 9 percent.” It shows that speeding dropped, not crashes. Only the police-records sentence measures crashes.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2 of his letter, Dunham writes that if the cameras become permanent, “soon there will be one on every corner of Ridgeview, watching where we go day and night.” Which kind of faulty reasoning is this?
items.explain: Dunham moves from one step (keeping two cameras on Lincoln Avenue) to an extreme result (a camera on every corner watching everyone day and night) and gives no evidence that the city plans or would allow this. That is a slippery slope. His letter also contains a bandwagon appeal (“Everyone on my street knows”) and a hasty generalization (one neighbor's ticket), but those are in paragraph 1, not in this sentence.
options: A slippery slope: it claims one step will lead to a far more extreme result, without evidence
A personal attack: it criticizes Brooks's character instead of responding to her evidence
A bandwagon appeal: it claims a position is right because many people already believe it
