A hasty generalization: it draws a broad rule from one person's single experience
why: Dunham never mentions Brooks or her character anywhere in his letter, so this is not a personal attack.
The bandwagon appeal is in paragraph 1: “Everyone on my street knows.” The sentence in paragraph 2 predicts a chain of events instead.
The hasty generalization is the neighbor's single ticket in paragraph 1. The sentence in paragraph 2 predicts where one step will lead.

items.prompt: Select two details from Dunham's letter that are examples of weak support.
items.explain: The neighbor's ticket is one example from one morning, too little to prove that the whole program is “a money grab” (a hasty generalization). “Everyone on my street knows” is a vague appeal to popular opinion with no source or numbers (bandwagon). The two points about mailed tickets and on-the-spot stops are Dunham's fairest arguments; a strong response would concede them and answer them with Brooks's evidence, not call them weak.
options: His neighbor's single $75 ticket, used to show that the cameras are a money grab
His statement that “Everyone on my street knows the cameras are about cash, not kids”
His point that a ticket arrives in the mail weeks after a driver has sped past
His point that a crossing guard or an officer can stop a dangerous driver on the spot
why: This is a reasonable point about how cameras work. A strong response would admit it and then note that Brooks's data shows speeding still fell from 41 to 9 percent.
This is a reasonable point, not weak support. It is also partly answered by Brooks, whose letter says ticket money pays for two crossing guards.

items.prompt:
Read the draft paragraph. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Sentence 3: The number of crashes in the zone also {{0}} from 14 to 6.

Sentence 4: {{1}} Dunham supports his claim with one ticket his neighbor received.

Sentence 5: One ticket on one morning cannot prove that the cameras are a money grab, and Dunham never explains how he knows what {{2}} neighbors think.
items.explain:
Sentence 3. The subject is “The number” (singular), not “crashes,” and the paragraph uses the past tense (“fell”), so the verb is dropped.

Sentence 4. The paragraph turns from Brooks's strong evidence to Dunham's weak evidence, so a contrast transition is needed: In contrast,.

Sentence 5. The neighbors belong to Dunham, so the possessive his is correct. “There,” “they're,” and “he's” are sound-alike or contraction errors.

options: dropped
drop
dropping
have dropped
why: “Drop” is plural and present tense. The subject is “The number,” which is singular, and the paragraph describes the trial in the past tense (“fell”).
“Dropping” cannot be the main verb. “The number of crashes also dropping” is a fragment.
“Have” is plural, but the subject is “The number,” not “crashes.” A singular subject would need “has,” and the paragraph is in the past tense.

options: In contrast,
Similarly,
As a result,
For example,
why: “Similarly,” says the two writers' evidence is alike. The paragraph is contrasting Brooks's measured results with Dunham's single ticket.
“As a result,” says Brooks's numbers caused Dunham's choice of evidence, which makes no sense.
“For example,” would introduce an example of the previous sentence's point, Brooks's crash data. Dunham's ticket is not an example of that.

options: his
there
they're
he's
why: “There” points to a place or starts a sentence. The neighbors belong to Dunham, so the possessive “his” is needed.
“They're” means “they are.” “What they are neighbors think” makes no sense.
“He's” means “he is” or “he has.” The sentence needs the possessive “his.”

items.prompt: The learner wants to add a final sentence to the draft paragraph that links back to the thesis. Which choice does this best?
items.explain: A strong final sentence (the “Link” in PEEL) ties the paragraph's evidence back to the thesis. “Because Brooks backs her claim with measured results and Dunham offers one ticket, Brooks's letter is the better supported” does exactly that. The concession about mailed tickets is tempting because it shows fairness, but placed here it weakens the paragraph's point; it belongs in its own concession paragraph that also answers it.
options: Because Brooks backs her claim with measured results and Dunham offers one ticket, Brooks's letter is the better supported.
Personally, I have never gotten a speeding ticket in a school zone, so I do not think the cameras are unfair to drivers at all.
Speed cameras are now used in many cities across the country, and more towns are likely to add them in the coming years.
Dunham does make a good point, though, that a ticket that arrives in the mail weeks later cannot stop a speeding driver.
why: This brings in the writer's own experience and opinion. A response judges the letters' support; it does not argue from personal experience.
This adds outside information that neither letter gives. A linking sentence ties the paragraph back to the thesis instead.
This is a concession. It could start a new paragraph, but ending this paragraph with it would undercut the point the paragraph just made.

items.prompt:
Read this learner's entire response to the speed-camera letters.

Brooks has numbers. Speeding went from 41 percent to 9 percent, and crashes went from 14 to 6. Dunham talks about his neighbor's ticket. Brooks also talks about privacy and says pictures are deleted within 30 days. Dunham says there will be cameras on every corner. Crossing guards are paid with the ticket money. Dunham says tickets come late.

Which revision would most improve this response's score on Trait 2 (development and organizational structure)?
items.explain: Trait 2 rewards a clear structure (introduction, body, conclusion), a logical progression of ideas, and transitions. This response is a list of accurate facts that jumps back and forth between the writers with no thesis, no paragraphs, no transitions, and no conclusion. Organizing it is the change that would most raise Trait 2. The “more facts” choice is tempting, but the response already has evidence; what it lacks is structure (and explanation, which is a Trait 1 issue).
options: Organize it into an introduction with a thesis, body paragraphs for each writer, and a conclusion, linked with transitions
Add two more facts from Brooks's letter, such as the length of the trial and the number of speed cameras that the city tested
Correct the grammar, spelling, and punctuation in every one of its sentences so that the response follows standard English
Add a sentence about the writer's own experience with speeding traffic near a school in the writer's neighborhood
why: More facts would affect Trait 1, and the response already has accurate details. Its problem is that the details are listed with no structure.
The sentences are already correct. Trait 3 is not the problem, and fixing nothing will not raise Trait 2.
Personal experience is off task, and adding it would make the list even less organized.

items.prompt: What does the passage suggest about how Denise's view of her résumé changes?
items.explain: At midnight, each stronger word (“trained,” “led”) “had felt like a small lie.” In the parking lot she remembers “each of the eleven: their names, their first clumsy weeks,” and Luis's first clean forklift backing. Those memories prove she really did train them. Her calm actions afterward (folding the résumé, checking the mirror, getting out of the car) show new confidence. The rewriting choice is tempting because she once felt the words were lies, but the passage shows that feeling changing, not growing.
options: At first the stronger words feel like exaggerations, but remembering the people she trained shows her they are accurate.
She decides that her résumé exaggerates her experience and makes up her mind to rewrite it before she goes inside.
She realizes in the parking lot that she forgot to list her forklift certification, so she quickly adds it at the last minute.
She becomes so nervous rereading the résumé that she considers driving home instead of going in for the interview.
why: This is contradicted. She folds the résumé, puts it in her bag, and gets out of the car, with no sign of rewriting it.
This is distorted. “Forklift certified” is already one of the lines she reads; nothing is added.
This is not supported. She checks her face in the mirror and gets out of the car; nothing suggests she thinks of leaving.

items.prompt: A learner is writing an Extended Response about the two school-uniform letters. Which thesis statement would best begin a high-scoring response?
items.explain: The prompt asks which position is better supported. The Hale thesis names the better-supported letter and previews reasons about evidence: measured referral and survey results and an answer to the cost concern, compared with one child's example and predictions. The “every student deserves the freedom” thesis is tempting because it sounds passionate, but it argues the issue instead of judging the letters.
options: Hale's letter is better supported because she reports measured results and answers the cost worry, while Lowe relies on his daughter and predictions.
Clearwater should not require uniforms, because every student deserves the freedom to show who they are and to design and wear the outfits that they love.
Hale and Lowe both care about Clearwater's middle school students, and each of their letters has some convincing points and some unconvincing ones.
This response will discuss two letters about school uniforms in Clearwater's middle schools and will summarize the main ideas that each writer presents.
why: This argues the issue (no uniforms) from the writer's own values. The task is to judge which letter is better supported, not which side is right.
This takes no position. Saying both letters have convincing and unconvincing points does not decide which is better supported.
This announces a summary. A thesis must make a judgment and preview the reasons.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from Hale's letter that gives the most specific evidence that families spent less on school clothes after Jefferson switched to uniforms.
items.explain: The question asks whether families spent less on school clothes. Only the survey sentence measures that: 71 percent of 280 families said they spent less after the change. “Uniforms also ease the pressure on family budgets” is the claim, not the evidence. The referral numbers are about discipline. The closet sentence answers a different worry, the cost of buying uniforms.
spans: The Clearwater school board should adopt uniforms at all three of its middle schools.
Jefferson Middle School switched to uniforms two years ago.
In the year before the change, the school recorded 312 discipline referrals.
In its second year with uniforms, it recorded 205.
Uniforms also ease the pressure on family budgets.
In a PTA survey answered by 280 Jefferson families, 71 percent said they spent less on school clothes after the change.
Some parents worry about the cost of buying uniforms.
Jefferson's uniform closet gives free uniforms to any family that asks, and last year it gave out 400 donated sets.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the uniform-closet sentence. The 400 donated sets show that free uniforms are available, but they do not measure whether families spent less on school clothes overall. The survey sentence does.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2 of his letter, Lowe writes, “Next the board will be telling our kids how to wear their hair and what to pack in their lunch boxes.” Which kind of faulty reasoning is this?
items.explain: Lowe moves from one step (uniform shirts and pants) to extreme results (rules about hair and lunch boxes) and offers no evidence that the board has proposed or would propose those rules. That is a slippery slope. The bandwagon appeal and the hasty generalization are both real weaknesses in his letter, but they appear in paragraph 1, not in this sentence.
options: A bandwagon appeal: it claims a position is right because many people already believe it
A slippery slope: it claims one step will lead to a far more extreme result, without evidence
A hasty generalization: it draws a broad rule from one person's single experience
A personal attack: it criticizes Hale's character instead of responding to her evidence
why: The bandwagon appeal is in paragraph 1: “Every parent I have talked to agrees.” This sentence predicts a chain of events instead.
The hasty generalization is the example of Lowe's daughter in paragraph 1. This sentence predicts where one step will lead.
Lowe never mentions Hale or her character, so this is not a personal attack.

items.prompt: Select two details from Lowe's letter that are examples of weak support.
items.explain: The daughter example is one child, too little to show how uniforms affect students across a district (a hasty generalization). “Every parent I have talked to agrees” is a vague appeal to popular opinion: he never says how many parents or who they are (bandwagon). The counselor point and the staff-list detail are Lowe's best support; they raise a fair question about what caused Jefferson's drop in referrals.
options: His point that Jefferson also hired a full-time counselor the same year it adopted uniforms
His example of his own daughter, who loves to design her own outfits
His statement that “Every parent I have talked to agrees that uniforms are a bad idea”
His note that the school's own staff list shows the counselor started that August
why: This is Lowe's strongest point. A second change at the same time makes it hard to know what caused the drop in referrals. A strong response would admit this and answer it.
This is specific, checkable evidence (the school's own staff list) that backs up his counselor point. It is a strength, not a weakness.

items.prompt:
Read the draft paragraph. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Sentence 3: A PTA survey of 280 families {{0}} that 71 percent spent less on school clothes.

Sentence 4: {{1}} Lowe supports his claim with the example of his own daughter.

Sentence 5: One child's love of designing outfits cannot show how uniforms affect a whole district, and Lowe never says how many parents {{2}} talked to.
items.explain:
Sentence 3. The subject is “A PTA survey” (singular), not “families,” and the survey happened in the past, so the verb is found.

Sentence 4. The paragraph turns from Hale's strong evidence to Lowe's weak evidence, so a contrast transition is needed: However,.

Sentence 5. The pronoun is the subject of “talked” and refers to Lowe, so it must be he.

options: found
find
finding
have found
why: “Find” is plural and present tense. The subject is “A PTA survey,” which is singular, and the survey was taken in the past.
“Finding” cannot be the main verb. “A PTA survey of 280 families finding that…” is a fragment.
“Have” is plural. The subject is “survey,” not “families,” so a plural verb does not agree.

options: However,
Likewise,
As a result,
In addition,
why: “Likewise,” says Lowe's evidence is similar to Hale's. The paragraph is contrasting her survey with his single example.
“As a result,” says Hale's survey caused Lowe's choice of evidence, which makes no sense.
“In addition,” adds another point of the same kind, but Lowe's daughter is not more evidence for Hale. The paragraph is turning to contrast.

options: he
him
he's
they
why: “Him” is an object pronoun. The pronoun here is the subject of “talked,” so it must be “he.”
“He's” means “he is” or “he has.” “How many parents he is talked to” is not correct English.
“They” would refer to more than one person, but the person doing the talking is Lowe, one man, so use “he.”

items.prompt: The learner wants to add a final sentence to the draft paragraph that links back to the thesis. Which choice does this best?
items.explain: The “Link” step of PEEL ties the paragraph's evidence back to the thesis. “Because Hale relies on school records and a survey while Lowe relies on one child, Hale's letter is the better supported” does that. The counselor concession is tempting because it is fair, but here it would weaken the paragraph's point; it belongs in a separate concession paragraph that also answers it.
options: Because Hale relies on school records and a survey while Lowe relies on one child, Hale's letter is the better supported.
When I was in middle school, I would have hated wearing a uniform every day, so I understand exactly how Lowe's daughter feels.
School uniforms have been common in many other countries for decades, and more American schools may require them in the future.
Lowe does raise a fair point, though, that Jefferson hired a full-time counselor in the same year that it adopted its uniforms.
why: This brings in the writer's personal feelings. A response judges the letters' support; it does not argue from the writer's own life.
This adds outside information that neither letter gives. A linking sentence ties the paragraph back to the thesis instead.
This is a concession. It belongs in its own paragraph with an answer; ending this paragraph with it undercuts the point just made.

items.prompt:
Read this learner's entire response to the school-uniform letters.

Hale says referrals went from 312 to 205. Lowe says his daughter likes to design her own outfits. Hale's survey says 71 percent of families spent less. The counselor was hired the same year. Lowe says every parent he talked to agrees with him. The uniform closet gave out 400 sets. Lowe thinks the board will make rules about hair.

Which revision would most improve this response's score on Trait 2 (development and organizational structure)?
items.explain: Trait 2 rewards a clear introduction, body, and conclusion, a logical progression of ideas, and transitions. This response lists accurate facts, jumping between the two writers with no thesis, no paragraphs, no transitions, and no conclusion. Organizing it is the change that would most raise Trait 2. Adding facts is tempting, but the response already has details; it needs structure (and explanation, which is a Trait 1 issue).
options: Organize it into an introduction with a thesis, body paragraphs for each writer, and a conclusion, linked with transitions
Add two more facts from Hale's letter, such as the number of families surveyed and the number of middle schools in Clearwater
Correct the grammar, spelling, and punctuation in every one of its sentences so that the response follows standard English
Add a sentence about what the writer wore to school and whether the writer's own school ever required uniforms
why: More facts would affect Trait 1, and the response already has accurate details. Its problem is that the details are listed with no structure.
The sentences are already correct. Trait 3 is not the problem, so this would not raise Trait 2.
Personal experience is off task, and adding it would make the list even less organized.

items.prompt: What does the mother's note mainly suggest about her?
items.explain: The note says, “For your first car. I'm keeping it for you,” and she leaves him the key to the cash box where the money is kept. She accepts his gesture but turns it into savings for his own goal, which shows pride and care. Her not touching the envelope earlier fits this: she lets the money be his. The “no interest” choice is tempting because she walks past the envelope twice, but the note shows the opposite.
options: She is proud of Marcus and wants to help him save for his own goal, not take his money.
She is angry that Marcus tried to pay her and wants him to know she does not need his help.
She needs the money for household bills and is quietly using it to cover the family's expenses.
She has no interest in Marcus's new job, which is why she walked past the envelope all evening.
why: This is not supported. Nothing in the note sounds angry; she keeps the money safe “for your first car” and gives him the key.
This is contradicted. The note says she is keeping the money for his first car, not spending it on bills.
This misreads her restraint. She walks past the envelope without touching it, which fits respect for his money, and her note shows she cares about his future.

vocab.def: The essay part of the GED RLA test, in which you analyze two arguments and explain which is better supported, in about 45 minutes.
vocab.example: The Extended Response asks which article uses stronger evidence.

vocab.def: One sentence that states your judgment about which argument is better supported and briefly why.
vocab.example: Okafor's argument is better supported because she uses measured results.

vocab.def: The opening paragraph that frames the issue, names both writers and their positions, and ends with the thesis.
vocab.example: Two writers disagree about whether job ads should list pay.

vocab.def: A middle paragraph that makes one point and supports it with specific, explained evidence.
vocab.example: A paragraph showing why Whitlock's anecdote is weak evidence.

vocab.def: The first sentence of a body paragraph, which states the paragraph's main point.
vocab.example: Whitlock's argument rests on much weaker support.

vocab.def: The final paragraph that restates the judgment in new words and sums up the reasons without adding new evidence.
vocab.example: In the end, Okafor makes the stronger case.

vocab.def: Exact facts, numbers, or words from a passage, credited to the writer.
vocab.example: The time to fill a job fell from 41 days to 33 days.

vocab.def: Naming the source of a quotation or idea.
A writer's exact words, placed in quotation marks.
Restating a writer's idea accurately in your own words.
vocab.example: Okafor says most pilot employers planned to keep posting pay.

vocab.def: Admitting that the other side has a fair point, then explaining why it does not change your judgment.
vocab.example: To be fair, the pilot employers volunteered; however, …

vocab.def: Improving the ideas, evidence, and organization of a draft.
vocab.example: Replacing a vague topic sentence with a clear point.

vocab.def: Correcting grammar, usage, spelling, capitalization, and punctuation.
A schedule that divides the time limit among reading, planning, drafting, and revising.
vocab.example: Read 8 minutes, plan 5, draft 25, revise and edit 7.

vocab.def: One of the three qualities GED scorers rate from 0 to 2: arguments and use of evidence; development and organization; clarity and command of standard English.
vocab.example: A clean essay with no passage evidence still scores low on Trait 1.

notes:
Week 10 RLA Study Sheet: The Extended Response II and Full Review

45-minute plan

MinTask
0–8Read prompt and passages; mark claims, evidence, weak spots
8–13Choose better-supported side; thesis; outline
13–38Draft: intro, 2–3 body paragraphs, conclusion
38–45Revise (3 min), edit (4 min)

Blueprint

  1. Intro: issue, both writers, thesis
  2. Body: stronger writer's evidence
  3. Body: weaker writer's evidence
  4. Body (optional): answer the weaker side's best point
  5. Conclusion: restate judgment; no new evidence

PEEL body paragraph

Point → Evidence → Explain → Link

Strong vs. weak evidence

  • Strong: measured results, records, named sources, answers to the other side
  • Weak: one story, predictions with no support, “many people say,” emotional appeals
  • Faulty reasoning: slippery slope, hasty generalization, personal attack, bandwagon

Last-minute edit list

  • Fragments, run-ons, comma splices
  • Subject-verb and pronoun agreement
  • their/there/they're; its/it's; then/than; to/too; a lot
  • Capitalize names and titles
  • Exact quotes and numbers

Full-review reminders

  • Reading: predict, match, prove. Traps: too narrow, too broad, not stated, distorted
  • Literary: trust actions over words
  • Drop-downs: read the whole sentence; find the real subject

Scoring traits (0–2 each): Trait 1, arguments and evidence. Trait 2, development and organization. Trait 3, clarity and standard English.

Low → middle → high: argues the issue or tells a personal story → judges the support but with vague evidence and empty explanation → specific, accurate evidence from both passages, explained, organized, with a concession.

Avoid: “I think”; arguing the issue instead of the support; quoting without explaining; skipping the weaker side; no conclusion; no edit.

Test day: pace by passage, answer every question, flag and return, and use every essay minute.
